laws.title: Límite de Alcohol — 0.5g/L
laws.subtitle: Reglamento Nacional de Tránsito
laws.fullDescription: Peru enforces a 0.5g/L BAC limit. Commercial vehicle drivers and motorcyclists have stricter limits. Police set up breathalyser checkpoints, especially on long weekends.
laws.penalty: Administrative sanction: licence suspension 1 year + fine. Criminal charges if accident caused.
exceptions: Commercial drivers: 0.0g/L
Motorcyclists: 0.0g/L

quiz.q: Peru's blood alcohol limit for private car drivers?
quiz.explanation: Peru's general BAC limit is 0.5g/L for private car drivers.

laws.title: Peruvian Culture — Warm, Proud, Community-Oriented
laws.subtitle: Respect for indigenous heritage; warmth in greetings
laws.fullDescription: Peruvians are warm and expressive. Handshake (men) or cheek kiss (women) on greeting. Peruvians are intensely proud of their cuisine (one of the world's best), Machu Picchu, and Inca heritage — engaging positively on these topics builds relationships. In highland indigenous communities, be respectful and ask permission before photographing people.
laws.penalty: No legal consequence — but disrespecting indigenous culture or refusing offered food causes offence.
exceptions: Lima (capital) is more cosmopolitan and formal
Highland communities have stricter traditional customs

quiz.q: What should you always ask before photographing people in Peruvian highland communities?
quiz.explanation: In Peruvian highland indigenous communities, always ask permission before taking photographs of people.

laws.title: Machu Picchu — Strict Access Rules and Conservation Laws
laws.subtitle: Ministry of Culture Res. — Timed entry tickets; touching ruins forbidden
laws.fullDescription: Machu Picchu is Peru's most visited site and has strict visitor management. Entry requires a timed ticket purchased in advance — spontaneous visits are not possible and tickets regularly sell out weeks ahead. Visitors must hire a licensed guide. Running, touching or climbing on the ruins is prohibited. Bringing in outside food and plastic bottles is restricted. The site can only be entered twice per day (morning and afternoon slots). Drones require a special permit from the Ministry of Culture — unauthorised drone use leads to serious fines and equipment confiscation.
laws.penalty: Entering without ticket: ejection + fine. Touching/climbing ruins: fine up to PEN 5,000. Drone without permit: confiscation + fine.
exceptions: Licensed archaeological teams with Ministry of Culture permits
Official conservation workers
laws.sourceLabel: Peru Ministry of Culture — Machu Picchu Regulations

quiz.q: Do you need to book Machu Picchu tickets in advance?
options: No — you can buy at the gate
Yes — timed tickets required; often sells out weeks ahead
Only if you want a guide
quiz.explanation: Machu Picchu requires pre-purchased timed entry tickets — visitors cannot buy tickets at the gate and slots regularly sell out weeks in advance, especially in peak season.

laws.title: Cannabis — Decriminalised; Personal Use Tolerated
laws.subtitle: Legislative Decree 1241 — Small amounts for personal use not prosecuted
laws.fullDescription: Peru decriminalised personal drug use in 1991 — possession of small amounts (up to 8g cannabis, 2g cocaine paste) for personal use is not prosecuted. However, trafficking, sale, or possession above personal thresholds is a serious criminal offence with lengthy prison sentences. The dividing line between 'personal use' and 'trafficking intent' is determined by prosecutors. Police corruption exists — travellers should be cautious of planted drugs scams. Medical cannabis was legalised in 2017.
laws.penalty: Possession above personal threshold: trafficking charge + 8–15 years imprisonment. Small personal amounts: not prosecuted (discretion applies).
exceptions: Medical cannabis: fully legal since 2017
Personal use threshold: up to 8g cannabis

quiz.q: What is Peru's personal cannabis possession threshold below which prosecution is unlikely?
quiz.explanation: Peru's drug law sets 8 grams as the threshold for cannabis — below this, personal use possession is typically not prosecuted, though police have discretion.

laws.title: Coca Leaf — Legal and Sacred in Peru; Illegal to Export
laws.subtitle: Andean cultural law — Coca is legal domestically; trafficking severe
laws.fullDescription: In Peru, coca leaves are legal to chew, brew into tea (mate de coca), and sell in markets — they are a sacred part of Andean culture and effective against altitude sickness. However, processing coca into cocaine is illegal, and exporting coca leaves without authorisation is a serious criminal offence under the Ley de Drogas. Peru is one of the world's largest coca producers — the drug trade is heavily monitored. At Machu Picchu and Cusco, coca tea is widely offered as a free welcome drink in hotels.
laws.penalty: Chewing or drinking coca tea: completely legal. Processing coca into cocaine: 8–15 years imprisonment. Exporting coca leaves: drug trafficking charges.
exceptions: Licensed pharmaceutical and traditional medicine producers
ENACO (National Coca Enterprise) for authorised commercial purposes
laws.sourceLabel: ENACO — Empresa Nacional de la Coca; Peru Drug Law

quiz.q: What is the legal status of coca leaves in Peru?
options: Legal to chew and drink as tea — a sacred Andean tradition
Only legal in the Amazon region
quiz.explanation: Coca leaves are completely legal in Peru — sacred to Andean culture and widely used as a tea to combat altitude sickness. However, exporting them is illegal and processing into cocaine carries heavy prison sentences.

laws.title: Machu Picchu Access Rules — UNESCO Preservation
laws.subtitle: Ministerio de Cultura — Timed entry; guided tours only in some areas
laws.fullDescription: Machu Picchu (UNESCO World Heritage Site) has strict visitor management rules. Since 2019, access is by timed entry tickets only — you must book in advance for a specific time slot. Entry is limited to around 3,000–4,500 visitors per day. The ruins are divided into circuits — visitors must follow the designated circuit and cannot roam freely. Climbing on the ruins, touching the stonework, or straying off paths is illegal. Bringing large bags, tripods, or umbrellas without special permits is prohibited. The Inca Trail requires advance permits (extremely limited) and must be done with a licensed agency.
laws.penalty: Touching or climbing ruins: ejection from site + possible fine. Off-circuit walking: ejection. Entering without timed ticket: denied entry.
exceptions: Licensed local guides have greater access for tour purposes
Researchers with Ministerio de Cultura permit
laws.sourceLabel: Ministerio de Cultura — Reglamento de Visitantes Machu Picchu

quiz.q: Since 2019, how must visitors access Machu Picchu?
options: Walk-up tickets at the gate on the day
By booking timed-entry tickets in advance for a specific slot
Only with an organised tour — no independent visits
quiz.explanation: Since 2019, Machu Picchu requires timed-entry tickets booked in advance — with daily limits of 3,000–4,500 visitors and designated circuits to protect the UNESCO site from over-tourism.

laws.title: Nazca Lines — No Off-Road; UNESCO Heritage; Strict Overflight Rules
laws.subtitle: Ministry of Culture — Ground access restricted; 2014 Greenpeace incident
laws.fullDescription: The Nazca Lines are ancient geoglyphs etched into the Peruvian desert — UNESCO World Heritage Site. Ground access is strictly controlled: the only legal way to view the lines at ground level is from a designated viewing platform (Mirador). Driving or walking on the pampa near the lines is a criminal offence — even small vehicles can destroy the fragile surface permanently. In 2014, Greenpeace activists left boot prints near the famous hummingbird geoglyph during a climate protest — Peru charged them with attacking cultural heritage. All aircraft overflying the lines must use licensed operators with Ministry of Transport-approved routes.
laws.penalty: Damaging or entering Nazca Lines pampa without authorisation: up to 4 years imprisonment + restitution under Law 28296. Unauthorised aircraft overflight: licence revocation + fine.
exceptions: Licensed tourist aircraft operators with Ministry of Transport certification
Ministry of Culture-authorised archaeological expeditions
laws.sourceLabel: Peruvian Ministry of Culture — Nazca Lines Regulations

quiz.q: In what year did Greenpeace activists controversially leave boot prints near the Nazca Lines?
quiz.explanation: In December 2014, Greenpeace activists entered the UNESCO-protected Nazca Lines pampa and left irreversible boot prints near the hummingbird geoglyph during a climate stunt — Peru charged them with attacking cultural heritage.

laws.title: Inti Raymi and Pachamama — Sacred Andean Festivals Have Specific Tourist Protocols
laws.subtitle: Ministry of Culture — Inti Raymi: ticket required; Pachamama offerings are sacred
laws.fullDescription: Peru celebrates Inti Raymi (Festival of the Sun) on June 24 each year in Cusco — a recreation of the Inca sun festival that draws thousands of tourists. The main ceremony at Sacsayhuamán fortress requires a paid ticket (around USD $100 for tourist seating) and attendance limits apply. More important to local Andean communities is Pachamama Day (August 1) — when offerings (pagos) to Mother Earth are made by shamans (paqos). These ceremonies are sacred and tourists are generally not invited to private family pagos without being introduced by a Cusco resident. The Ministry of Culture's 2021 regulation requires all tour operators at Inca sites to employ at least one certified Peruvian guide.
laws.penalty: Entering Sacsayhuamán without a ticket on Inti Raymi: ejection. Disrupting a Pachamama ceremony: serious cultural offence — police may be called.
exceptions: Invited guests of Peruvian families for private Pachamama ceremonies
Press with Ministry of Culture media accreditation for Inti Raymi
laws.sourceLabel: Peruvian Ministry of Culture — Inti Raymi and Andean Heritage

quiz.q: On what date is Inti Raymi (Festival of the Sun) celebrated each year in Cusco, Peru?
quiz.explanation: Inti Raymi is celebrated on June 24 each year in Cusco — near the June winter solstice in the Southern Hemisphere (the shortest day in Peru), which the Inca considered the moment when the Sun God (Inti) needed to be honoured to return.

laws.title: Machu Picchu Carrying Capacity — Timed Entry; Strict Visitor Limits Enforced
laws.subtitle: Peru caps daily visitors to Machu Picchu at 5,940; passport required for entry
laws.fullDescription: UNESCO's concerns about over-tourism at Machu Picchu (inscribed 1983) prompted Peru's Ministry of Culture to implement strict carrying capacity limits. Since 2017, maximum daily visitors are capped at 5,940 (previously unlimited). Entry is divided into morning (6:00–12:00) and afternoon (12:00–17:30) shifts, each with a capacity cap. Visitors must specify which circuit (1, 2, or 3) they will follow — changing circuits inside is prohibited. Passports must match the tickets (non-transferable). High-demand dates sell out months in advance. Hiking Huayna Picchu or Machu Picchu Mountain requires separate, more limited tickets (400 per day for Huayna Picchu). The Classic Inca Trail requires permits booked up to a year in advance — limited to 500 people daily including guides and porters.
laws.penalty: Entering without valid time-slot ticket: immediate ejection without refund. Unauthorized trail use: fines + ejection from site. Damaging site elements: criminal charges under Peruvian Cultural Heritage Law.
exceptions: UNESCO emergency conservation teams
Peruvian residents with national ID card get discounted tickets but same time restrictions
Scientific research teams with Ministry of Culture permits
laws.sourceLabel: Peruvian Ministry of Culture — Machu Picchu Visitor Regulations

quiz.q: How many daily visitors are currently allowed at Machu Picchu under Peru's carrying capacity rules?
options: Unlimited — only circuit routing is controlled
quiz.explanation: Peru caps Machu Picchu visitors at 5,940 per day, divided between morning and afternoon sessions. This limit was established after UNESCO concerns about over-tourism — previously, up to 10,000+ visitors per day were creating serious deterioration risks to the site.

laws.title: Las Bambas Mining Conflict — Indigenous Consultation Rights vs. Mining Company Interests
laws.subtitle: Peru's Las Bambas copper mine has faced hundreds of days of blockades over ILO 169 consultation failures
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Las Bambas copper mine (one of the world's largest, operated by China's MMG Limited) has faced extraordinary community opposition since 2015 — over 300 days of road blockades that have cost billions in production losses. At issue: Peru ratified ILO Convention 169 (Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention, 1989) which requires free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC) for projects affecting Indigenous communities. However, the project's Environmental Impact Assessment changed multiple times (route changes, processing method changes) without new consultations. The Peruvian government has repeatedly declared states of emergency in the corridor. The Añañi and Chumbivilcas communities demand direct revenue-sharing. Peru's Constitutional Tribunal has interpreted ILO 169 as requiring consultation but not necessarily veto rights.
laws.penalty: Mining without required consultation: mine suspension orders + legal challenges before Constitutional Tribunal. Community blockades (under criminal law): terrorism or obstruction charges — contested as criminalizing protest.
exceptions: Emergency measures for national security with presidential authorization
Projects with completed and valid ILO 169 consultation processes
Small-scale artisanal mining in designated zones with different consultation requirements
laws.sourceLabel: Peruvian Ministry of Energy and Mines — ILO 169 Consultation Framework

quiz.q: What international convention guarantees Indigenous peoples the right to free, prior, and informed consent for projects affecting their lands?
options: UN DRIP (Declaration on Rights of Indigenous Peoples) 2007
quiz.explanation: ILO Convention 169 (1989) on Indigenous and Tribal Peoples requires states to consult with Indigenous communities and obtain their free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC) for projects affecting their lands. Peru ratified ILO 169 — but implementation gaps, particularly around project changes mid-construction, have driven the Las Bambas mining conflicts.

laws.title: Forced Sterilization Crimes (1996–2000)
laws.subtitle: Fujimori-era campaign forcibly sterilized 270,000+ indigenous women
laws.fullDescription: Between 1996 and 2000, Peru's government under Alberto Fujimori implemented the Voluntary Surgical Contraception Program (PNSRPF), which forcibly sterilized an estimated 270,000–300,000 women — predominantly indigenous Quechua-speaking women in rural areas — without informed consent. Women were coerced with food or threatened with fines. Many died from botched procedures. Fujimori, who served prison time for other crimes, died in 2023 before facing trial for sterilizations. A 2024 constitutional tribunal ruling declared the forced sterilizations a crime against humanity, and the state agreed to compensate survivors.
laws.penalty: Criminal charges against state officials remain contested; the case was closed and reopened multiple times. In 2024, courts found the state liable. Fujimori died without facing sterilization charges.
exceptions: Survivors registered in REINFO database are eligible for reparations
Children of victims can also receive compensation
Cases remain active in Inter-American Court of Human Rights

quiz.q: How many women were estimated to have been forcibly sterilized under Peru's Fujimori-era program?
quiz.explanation: The Fujimori government's 1996–2000 sterilization program forcibly sterilized an estimated 270,000–300,000 women, mostly indigenous Quechua-speaking women, declared a crime against humanity in 2024.

laws.title: Dina Boluarte Presidency & Protest Killings
laws.subtitle: Peru's sixth president in six years oversaw security forces killing 49 protesters in January 2023
laws.fullDescription: After President Pedro Castillo's self-coup attempt and immediate removal from office (December 2022), Vice President Dina Boluarte assumed the presidency. Protests — primarily from Indigenous and rural communities in southern Peru who had voted for Castillo — were met with lethal force: 49 protesters were killed in January 2023, including children. The Ayacucho and Puno massacres triggered international condemnation. Peru has had six presidents in six years (2017–2023), reflecting extreme political instability. Boluarte's government faced corruption investigations; her jewelry of unexplained origin (the 'Rolexgate' scandal) triggered further protests in 2024.
laws.penalty: Security forces who killed protesters face criminal investigation under international humanitarian law. Protest organizers charged with terrorism faced preventive detention. Obstruction of investigations: criminal charges.
exceptions: Inter-American Commission on Human Rights opened precautionary measures for Peru
Prosecutorial immunity for serving president complicates investigations against Boluarte
Congressional immunity has historically protected Peruvian legislators from prosecution
laws.sourceLabel: Inter-American Court of Human Rights — Peru

quiz.q: How many presidents has Peru had between 2017 and 2023?
quiz.explanation: Peru had six presidents in six years between 2017 and 2023 — reflecting extreme political instability driven by conflicts between executive and legislative branches, impeachments, resignations, and a self-coup attempt.

laws.title: Machu Picchu Tourist Caps & UNESCO Pressure
laws.subtitle: Peru implemented strict visitor limits at Machu Picchu after UNESCO threatened to list it as 'in danger'
laws.fullDescription: Machu Picchu, the 15th-century Inca citadel and Peru's most visited site, has faced a decade-long battle over overcrowding. UNESCO repeatedly warned that excessive tourism was damaging the site. In 2023, Peru implemented strict entrance controls: timed entry tickets (no more standing in lines), a daily cap of 5,600 visitors (up from the previous 3,044), and mandatory guides for all visitors. In 2022, protests by tourism workers against a competing entrance near Aguas Calientes briefly shut the site. Peru earns $1+ billion annually from Machu Picchu tourism — making conservation vs. revenue a permanent tension.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized entry without a ticket: removal and fine. Damage to Inca stonework: criminal prosecution. Tour operators who exceed licensed group sizes: license suspension.
exceptions: Peruvian citizens pay reduced entrance fees (approximately 50% discount)
Scientific researchers receive free access for registered projects
Sunrise visits for spiritual ceremonies may be permitted for indigenous communities with advance approval

quiz.q: What is the current daily visitor limit at Machu Picchu implemented in 2023?
quiz.explanation: Peru implemented a daily cap of 5,600 visitors at Machu Picchu in 2023 with timed entry tickets and mandatory guides — a measure responding to UNESCO's warnings about overcrowding damage, though the cap is higher than the previous 3,044 limit that critics argued was already too large.

laws.title: Fujimori's Pardons & the Fight Over Amnesty for Human Rights Criminals
laws.subtitle: Peru's courts repeatedly cancelled Alberto Fujimori's humanitarian pardon — a battle over impunity for mass killings that outlasted Fujimori himself
laws.fullDescription: Former Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori (1990–2000) was convicted in 2009 of crimes against humanity for the Barrios Altos and La Cantuta massacres committed by the Grupo Colina death squad, receiving a 25-year sentence. In December 2017, President Kuczynski granted Fujimori a 'humanitarian' pardon — widely seen as political payback for Fujimori's son Kenji delivering parliamentary votes to save Kuczynski from impeachment. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights suspended the pardon. It was reinstated by the Constitutional Tribunal in 2023. Fujimori was released and died in September 2024. His legacy remains deeply divisive between those who credit him for defeating Shining Path terrorism and those who see him as a war criminal.
laws.penalty: Fujimori's original 25-year sentence for crimes against humanity. His final release and subsequent death made the legal battle moot, but the precedent remains contested
exceptions: The Inter-American Court's jurisdiction to supervise compliance with convictions was itself contested by Peru's Constitutional Tribunal
Fujimori's daughter Keiko has her own separate corruption prosecutions
laws.sourceLabel: Inter-American Court of Human Rights – Fujimori

quiz.q: For what crimes was Alberto Fujimori convicted in 2009?
options: Crimes against humanity for death squad massacres
quiz.explanation: Alberto Fujimori was convicted in 2009 of crimes against humanity for the Barrios Altos and La Cantuta massacres carried out by the Grupo Colina death squad during his presidency — receiving a landmark 25-year sentence.

laws.title: Peru's Political Chaos: 6 Presidents in 5 Years & Castillo's Self-Coup
laws.subtitle: Peru went through six presidents in five years — including Pedro Castillo, who attempted a self-coup by dissolving congress before being arrested
laws.fullDescription: Peru's political system has been in near-continuous crisis: between 2016 and 2023, the country had six presidents. Pedro Castillo, a rural schoolteacher elected on a leftist platform in 2021, faced two impeachment attempts before attempting his own escape: on December 7, 2022, he announced he was dissolving Congress and establishing an 'emergency government' — an action the Constitutional Tribunal immediately ruled illegal. Within hours, Congress impeached him and police arrested him. His VP, Dina Boluarte, became Peru's first female president. Deadly protests erupted in southern Peru demanding her resignation and new elections; over 60 protesters were killed by security forces. Peru's constitution allows Congress to remove presidents under a vague 'moral incapacity' clause.
laws.penalty: Castillo: rebellion and other charges carrying up to 35 years imprisonment. Anti-Boluarte protesters faced tear gas and live fire; some were charged with terrorism
exceptions: The 'moral incapacity' constitutional provision for presidential removal has no precise legal definition — each case is essentially political
Peru's Constitutional Tribunal has authority to review but not reverse congressional impeachment decisions

quiz.q: What unprecedented action did Peru's President Castillo take on December 7, 2022 before being arrested?
options: He announced dissolution of Congress and an emergency government — a self-coup attempt
quiz.explanation: Castillo announced he was dissolving Congress and establishing an 'emergency government' — a blatant self-coup attempt — which the Constitutional Tribunal immediately ruled illegal. Congress impeached him within hours and he was arrested while apparently trying to flee to the Mexican embassy.

laws.title: Machu Picchu Visitor Cap Law
laws.subtitle: Peru limits daily visitors to Machu Picchu to protect the ancient site
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Ministry of Culture enforces a daily visitor limit at Machu Picchu of 4,044 people (as of 2023 regulations), spread across two time slots to reduce crowding at the 15th-century Inca citadel. Entry requires advance ticket purchase, timed entry slots, and a licensed guide for certain areas. UNESCO designated Machu Picchu a World Heritage Site in 1983 and has repeatedly raised concerns about over-tourism. After COVID-19 restored the site (previously receiving 5,000+ daily visitors), Peru used the recovery period to redesign the access system. Unauthorized entry, including via the 'Inca Trail' without permits, results in fines and expulsion.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized entry: fines; unlicensed guiding: fines and professional license suspension; climbing restricted structures: criminal charges
exceptions: Scientific research missions can access restricted areas with Ministry permits
Local Peruvian residents from Aguas Calientes have discounted entry

quiz.q: How many daily visitors are now permitted at Machu Picchu?
quiz.explanation: Peru's current regulations cap daily visitors at Machu Picchu at 4,044 people split across two time slots — a significant reduction from the pre-COVID peak of over 5,000 daily visitors that threatened the site's structural integrity.

laws.title: Amazon Indigenous Territorial Rights
laws.subtitle: Peru recognizes indigenous territorial rights in its Amazon basin communities
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Law 22175 (Communities Law, 1978) and ILO Convention 169 (ratified 1994) recognize the territorial rights of indigenous Amazonian communities (comunidades nativas). Communities with recognized territorial titles hold inalienable, imprescriptible rights to their ancestral territories. However, the Peruvian state retains ownership of subsoil resources (oil, gas, minerals), creating fundamental conflict between indigenous territorial rights and extractive industry permits. The 2009 Bagua Massacre — in which police clashed with indigenous protesters blockading roads against oil industry legislation, killing at least 33 people — became a watershed moment for indigenous rights.
laws.penalty: Invading recognized indigenous territories: criminal trespass; unauthorized resource extraction: criminal charges under environmental law
exceptions: Prior consultation (consulta previa) under ILO 169 is required before resource extraction in indigenous territories — though compliance is inconsistent
laws.sourceLabel: Peruvian Ministry of Culture – Indigenous Peoples

quiz.q: What tragic 2009 event became a watershed moment for indigenous rights in Peru?
options: The Madre de Dios gold rush
quiz.explanation: The Bagua Massacre of June 2009 occurred when Peruvian police forcibly removed indigenous protesters blocking a road in the Amazon. At least 33 people were killed. It led to the repeal of the contested oil and gas laws and galvanized Peru's indigenous rights movement.

laws.title: Mining Conflict Law
laws.subtitle: Peru's Law 29785 requires prior consultation with indigenous communities before mining projects
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Law 29785 (Prior Consultation Law, 2011) implements ILO Convention 169, requiring the state to consult with indigenous peoples before approving extractive industry projects in their territories. Peru has the most mining conflicts of any Latin American country — over 200 active conflicts documented by the Ombudsman. Major conflicts include Conga (Cajamarca), Tía María (Arequipa), and Las Bambas (Apurímac). Protests over mining have led to multiple states of emergency and hundreds of deaths since 2000. Despite the Prior Consultation Law, indigenous communities argue consultations are often inadequate and mining proceeds over their objections.
laws.penalty: Mining companies that proceed without completing consultation processes face judicial injunctions and administrative sanctions; police and military deployed to protect mining operations — protesters face criminal charges for obstruction
exceptions: Projects authorized before the 2011 law are not retroactively subject to prior consultation
Emergency infrastructure projects can proceed with accelerated consultations
laws.sourceLabel: Peru Ministry of Culture – Prior Consultation

quiz.q: How many active mining conflicts did Peru's Ombudsman document?
quiz.explanation: Peru's Ombudsman (Defensoría del Pueblo) documented over 200 active social conflicts — most related to mining — making Peru the country with the most extractive industry conflicts in Latin America. Disputes typically involve water contamination fears, land rights, and inadequate prior consultation.

laws.title: Presidential Impeachment Crisis and Institutional Instability
laws.subtitle: Peru has had six presidents in five years, driven by repeated use of 'moral incapacity' impeachment
laws.fullDescription: Peru has experienced extraordinary political instability: between 2016 and 2023, the country had six different presidents. The constitutional mechanism of 'moral incapacity' (Article 113(2) of the 1993 Constitution) allows Congress to remove a president by a two-thirds vote for 'permanent moral incapacity' — a term the constitution does not define. This vague standard has been weaponized: Pedro Pablo Kuczynski resigned under impeachment threat (2018); Martín Vizcarra was removed by Congress (November 2020) in a vote widely criticized as a coup by legislature; Manuel Merino resigned after massive protests following his 5-day presidency; Francisco Sagasti completed the term; and Pedro Castillo (elected 2021) attempted a self-coup in December 2022 (dissolving Congress by decree), was immediately impeached and arrested; Dina Boluarte became president. Peru's political system suffers from a fundamental conflict between a fragmented, corruption-prone legislature and executive.
laws.penalty: A removed president loses immunity and can be prosecuted; Pedro Castillo faces multiple corruption and coup charges; Peru's Attorney General and Constitutional Tribunal oversee the legal framework
exceptions: A sitting president with immunity cannot be prosecuted while in office (except for treason and specific crimes)
The Constitutional Tribunal can review whether 'moral incapacity' was properly applied
Amnesty laws periodically affect accountability for political crimes

laws.title: Alberto Fujimori Pardon and Constitutional Crisis
laws.subtitle: The pardon of Alberto Fujimori for crimes against humanity triggered a major constitutional dispute
laws.fullDescription: Former Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori (1990-2000) was convicted in 2009 for human rights violations including the Barrios Altos massacre and La Cantuta killings (carried out by the Grupo Colina death squad) and sentenced to 25 years imprisonment — one of the first times a democratically elected head of state was convicted of human rights crimes by his own country's courts. President Pedro Pablo Kuczynski granted Fujimori a 'humanitarian pardon' in December 2017 (widely seen as a political deal for political support). The Inter-American Court of Human Rights ordered Peru to annul the pardon, finding it violated victims' rights to justice. Peru's Supreme Court annulled the pardon in 2022. However, Peru's Constitutional Tribunal reinstated it in a controversial 4-3 ruling in March 2022. Fujimori was released. He passed away in September 2024. His daughter Keiko Fujimori has continued the Fujimorismo political movement and faced her own corruption charges.
laws.penalty: The original conviction: 25 years imprisonment (served in part); annulment proceedings: legal dispute between Constitutional Tribunal and Supreme Court
exceptions: The Inter-American Court of Human Rights' rulings create binding international obligations for Peru
Victims retained the right to civil reparations regardless of pardon status
The pardoned crimes involved military defendants who faced separate proceedings

laws.title: Boluarte's Presidency and Deadly Protests
laws.subtitle: Peru's succession crisis left a fragile government facing mass protests
laws.fullDescription: In December 2022, Peru's Congress impeached President Pedro Castillo moments after he attempted to dissolve Congress unconstitutionally. Vice President Dina Boluarte assumed the presidency. Protests — particularly in southern, indigenous regions — erupted, demanding new elections and a new constitution. Security forces killed at least 49 protesters. Boluarte was investigated for genocide and human rights violations. Meanwhile, Congress passed laws considered to benefit accused criminals and delayed elections. Peru has had 6 presidents in under 6 years, reflecting chronic institutional instability. Boluarte's government remained in power but faced continuous impeachment threats and low approval ratings.
laws.penalty: Unconstitutional dissolution of Congress: immediate removal from office under Article 134. Protesting without permit in designated zones: administrative detention.
exceptions: Constitutional right to protest protected under Article 2(12)
Congress has limited grounds for presidential removal under incapacity provisions

quiz.q: How did Dina Boluarte become Peru's president?
options: She won a snap election called after Castillo resigned
She was vice president and assumed office when Congress impeached Castillo
She was appointed by the Constitutional Tribunal
She won a runoff against Castillo
quiz.explanation: Boluarte became president when Congress impeached Pedro Castillo minutes after he attempted to dissolve Congress unconstitutionally — a self-coup attempt that triggered his immediate removal.

laws.title: Rolex-gate – Boluarte's Luxury Watch Scandal
laws.subtitle: Peru's president faced investigation over undisclosed luxury watches
laws.fullDescription: Peru's President Dina Boluarte faced a major corruption scandal in early 2024 when she was found to be wearing expensive luxury watches — Rolex models worth tens of thousands of dollars — that she had not declared in her public asset statements as required by Peruvian law. Prosecutors raided the presidential palace and her brother's home. Boluarte claimed the watches were loaned by friends. Prosecutors investigated for illicit enrichment and failure to declare assets. The scandal became known as 'Rolex-gate' and drove her approval ratings below 5% — among the lowest of any sitting head of state globally. Despite impeachment threats, she survived due to congressional dynamics, but the scandal symbolized Peru's chronic governance crisis.
laws.penalty: Illicit enrichment by public official: up to 8 years imprisonment under Peruvian anti-corruption law. Failure to declare assets: up to 4 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Gifts below a threshold value from foreign heads of state may be retained
Loaned items not owned may not trigger asset declaration requirements — Boluarte's defense

quiz.q: What became known as 'Rolex-gate' in Peru?
options: A scandal over government contracts with Swiss watchmakers
President Boluarte wearing undeclared luxury Rolex watches not in her public asset declaration
A tax evasion scheme involving watch importers
The theft of a historic Rolex from the presidential palace
quiz.explanation: 'Rolex-gate' referred to the discovery that President Boluarte was wearing expensive Rolex watches worth tens of thousands of dollars that she had not declared in mandatory public asset statements — triggering a presidential palace raid and corruption investigation.

laws.title: Peru's Congress and Narco-Politics Scandal
laws.subtitle: Peru's Congress was accused of links to drug trafficking and human trafficking networks
laws.fullDescription: Peru's political crisis deepened in 2024 with investigations revealing alleged links between members of Congress and criminal organizations. Prosecutors investigated alleged relationships between legislators and narco-trafficking groups operating in the VRAEM (Valley of the Apurímac, Ene and Mantaro Rivers) — Peru's main coca production zone. The term 'narcopolítica' (narco-politics) became common in Peruvian political discourse. The Constitutional Tribunal and Judiciary faced allegations of being improperly influenced. Peru's National Police corruption issues also surfaced. The International Narcotics Control Board highlighted Peru as a concern. Peru has consistently been among the world's top three coca producers alongside Colombia and Bolivia.
laws.penalty: Narco-financing of political parties: up to 15 years imprisonment under anti-corruption law. Money laundering linked to drug trafficking: up to 25 years.
exceptions: Traditional coca use and small-scale cultivation in designated legal areas permitted under Peruvian law
ENACO (state coca company) licenses legitimate coca for traditional and industrial use

quiz.q: What is the VRAEM in Peru?
options: A special economic zone for legal coca processing
The Valley of the Apurímac, Ene and Mantaro Rivers — Peru's main coca production zone
A national park in the Andes protected from mining
An acronym for Peru's counter-narcotics task force
quiz.explanation: VRAEM (Valley of the Apurímac, Ene and Mantaro Rivers) is the main coca-producing region in Peru and a stronghold of Sendero Luminoso remnants (Shining Path) — one of the world's most significant drug-producing areas and a persistent governance and security challenge.

laws.title: Peru's Boluarte Government and Anti-Protest Crackdowns
laws.subtitle: Castillo removal and deadly crackdowns on southern Peru protests
laws.fullDescription: Following the impeachment and arrest of President Pedro Castillo in December 2022, Peru descended into its worst political crisis in decades. Protesters — primarily from the poorer indigenous south — demanded new elections, a new constitution, and the resignation of President Dina Boluarte. Security forces killed at least 49 protesters. Boluarte declared multiple states of emergency granting expanded military powers. The protests highlighted deep divisions between Lima and indigenous southern regions. Peru's Congress repeatedly extended emergency powers while blocking early elections that protesters demanded.
laws.penalty: Protest-related charges: terrorism, sedition, assault on security forces (5-25 years). State of emergency violations: arrest and detention. Participating in 'unauthorized' assemblies during emergency: up to 2 years. Security forces using lethal force: internal investigations with limited accountability
exceptions: Indigenous communities have constitutional right to prior consultation on resource projects
Peaceful assembly rights technically maintained but emergency measures override them
International human rights monitoring organizations have access in principle

quiz.q: How many protesters were killed during the 2022-2023 unrest following Pedro Castillo's removal in Peru?
quiz.explanation: At least 49 protesters were killed during the political crisis following President Castillo's removal in December 2022, with security forces using lethal force against demonstrations primarily in Peru's southern indigenous communities.

laws.title: Peru's Amazon Deforestation and Illegal Mining Crisis
laws.subtitle: Illegal gold mining destroys Amazon while government struggles to enforce law
laws.fullDescription: Peru is the world's third largest gold producer, but illegal artisanal gold mining (known as 'minería ilegal' or 'ASGM') in regions like Madre de Dios has devastated Amazon rainforest — destroying over 100,000 hectares with mercury contamination and deforestation. Mercury used in gold extraction contaminates rivers and accumulates in fish, affecting indigenous communities. Peru's government has conducted Operation Mercurio and other crackdowns but struggles with corruption in enforcement. The Environmental Evaluation and Inspection Agency (OEFA) monitors compliance. Mercury use in ASGM was banned by decree but enforcement is limited.
laws.penalty: Illegal mining: up to 10 years imprisonment plus remediation costs. Mercury use in mining: up to 8 years. Environmental damage in Amazon buffer zones: up to 15 years. Laundering illegal mining proceeds: up to 12 years. Corrupt officials facilitating illegal mining: up to 15 years
exceptions: Formalized small-scale artisanal miners in approved zones can operate legally
Indigenous community members have some rights to traditional resource use
Research and monitoring activities permitted in affected areas
laws.sourceLabel: Peru Environmental Evaluation and Inspection Agency

quiz.q: What heavy metal used in illegal Amazon gold mining contamination is particularly dangerous to health?
quiz.explanation: Mercury is used in illegal artisanal gold mining to amalgamate gold particles, then burned off — contaminating rivers and accumulating in fish through bioaccumulation. Indigenous communities in Peru's Madre de Dios region show dangerous mercury levels in their blood from consuming contaminated fish.

laws.title: Illegal Mining Enforcement in Protected Areas
laws.subtitle: Peru criminalizes illegal gold mining destroying Amazon ecosystems
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Legislative Decree 1100 and subsequent laws criminalize illegal mining (minería ilegal) in protected natural areas, river buffer zones, and indigenous territories. The Madre de Dios region has suffered massive deforestation from illegal gold mining. Environmental prosecutors and specialized units conduct raids, destroy illegal equipment, and prosecute mine operators. Mercury contamination from illegal gold processing is an additional environmental crime. Purchasing gold from illegal mining operations also carries criminal liability under anti-money-laundering laws. Formalization programs allow some small-scale miners to obtain legal status.
laws.penalty: Illegal mining in protected areas: 4–12 years imprisonment; using mercury illegally: additional 4–8 years
exceptions: Formally registered small-scale artisanal mining within permitted zones
Traditional indigenous subsistence panning (limited exemption)

quiz.q: What environmental crime accompanies illegal gold mining in Peru's Madre de Dios region?
quiz.explanation: Illegal gold mining in Peru's Amazon regions, especially Madre de Dios, causes massive mercury contamination from the gold amalgamation process, constituting an additional environmental crime.

laws.title: Presidential Impeachment and Constitutional Vacancy
laws.subtitle: Peru has removed multiple presidents using 'moral incapacity' constitutional provision
laws.fullDescription: Peru's constitution contains an unusual provision allowing Congress to remove a president for 'permanent moral incapacity' — a vague standard used to remove three presidents since 2016 (Kuczynski, Vizcarra, and Castillo). Pedro Castillo's 2022 removal followed his attempt to dissolve Congress unconstitutionally and seize power; his vice president Dina Boluarte became president amid massive protests. Peru's high court has reviewed impeachment cases. The repeated use of moral incapacity removal has been criticized as enabling legislative coups. Peru's political instability has significantly impacted foreign investment, particularly in the mining sector.
laws.penalty: Attempting to dissolve Congress unconstitutionally: criminal prosecution for rebellion; coup attempts: up to 15 years imprisonment
exceptions: Normal legislative oversight and confidence votes in prime minister use different procedures
Constitutional impeachment through supermajority vote is a separate legitimate process

quiz.q: What vague constitutional provision has Peru used to remove multiple presidents?
quiz.explanation: Peru's constitutional provision of 'permanent moral incapacity' has been used to remove three presidents since 2016, drawing criticism that its vague standard enables Congress to remove presidents for political rather than genuine incapacity reasons.

laws.title: Mining Protests and Community Consultation Laws
laws.subtitle: Peru's free prior and informed consent requirements for mining projects remain contested
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Law 29785 (Free Prior and Informed Consultation Law, 2011) implements ILO Convention 169, requiring consultation with indigenous communities before projects affecting their territories. However, implementation has been deeply contested. Mining projects have been blocked or delayed by consultation disputes. Las Bambas copper mine, one of Peru's largest, has experienced repeated road blockades by affected communities. The government has declared states of emergency around key mining projects. Peru's Defensoría del Pueblo (Ombudsman) mediates social conflicts. The legal framework for consultation is clear in theory but enforcement and good-faith implementation by companies and government remain inconsistent.
laws.penalty: Proceeding with mining project without completing required consultation: court injunctions and project suspension; violations during consultation: administrative sanctions
exceptions: Emergency mining operations related to safety can proceed with concurrent consultation
Infrastructure maintenance on existing projects has simplified requirements

quiz.q: What law implements ILO Convention 169 on indigenous consultation rights in Peru?
quiz.explanation: Peru's Law 29785, the Free Prior and Informed Consultation Law (2011), implements ILO Convention 169 requiring consultation with indigenous communities before projects affecting their territories — a law whose implementation remains highly contested in practice.

laws.title: Peru Political Crisis and Constitutional Law Changes
laws.subtitle: Peru faces recurring impeachments and constitutional challenges
laws.fullDescription: Peru has experienced significant political instability with multiple presidential impeachments and constitutional crises. Following the failed self-coup by Pedro Castillo in December 2022 and his subsequent arrest, Congress granted itself expanded impeachment powers. Legal debates continue over the threshold for moral incapacity as grounds for presidential removal. The Constitutional Tribunal has been called upon repeatedly to adjudicate disputes between Congress and the executive branch.
laws.penalty: Impeached officials lose office and may face criminal charges; contempt of court carries imprisonment
exceptions: Acts taken under valid presidential emergency powers
Legislative immunity for congressional votes
Diplomatic immunity for foreign representatives

quiz.q: What controversial ground has Peru's Congress used to impeach presidents?
options: Moral incapacity as a broad constitutional ground
quiz.explanation: Peru's Congress has repeatedly invoked moral incapacity as a vague constitutional provision to impeach presidents, leading to significant political instability.

laws.title: Peru Mining Conflicts and Indigenous Consultation Law
laws.subtitle: Peru requires prior consultation with indigenous communities for mining projects
laws.fullDescription: Peru has implemented the Prior Consultation Law (Law 29785) based on ILO Convention 169, requiring the state to consult with indigenous communities before approving projects that affect their territories. Despite the law, Peru has experienced frequent social conflicts around mining projects. The Constitutional Tribunal has ruled on multiple cases defining consultation rights. The government has also used states of emergency to manage mining-related protests, creating tensions between development priorities and indigenous rights.
laws.penalty: Projects approved without required prior consultation face court challenge and suspension; violation of consultation rights: administrative penalties for the state
exceptions: Small artisanal mining by community members themselves
Infrastructure projects in non-indigenous territories
Emergency resource extraction under declared national emergency
laws.sourceLabel: Peru Ministry of Energy and Mines

quiz.q: On what international instrument is Peru's Prior Consultation Law based?
options: UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
The Inter-American Convention on Human Rights
quiz.explanation: Peru's Prior Consultation Law (Law 29785) is based on ILO Convention 169 (Convention concerning Indigenous and Tribal Peoples), which requires governments to consult indigenous communities before approving development projects affecting their territories.

laws.title: Peru Mining and Oil Block Protests — Social Conflict Law
laws.subtitle: Peru manages pervasive social conflicts around extractive industries
laws.fullDescription: Peru leads Latin America in mining-related social conflicts, with hundreds of active conflicts between extractive companies and communities recorded by the Ombudsman's office. The government has developed a framework for managing social conflict through dialogue tables, early warning systems, and mandatory community engagement. However, protests have escalated at multiple sites including Las Bambas copper mine, which has faced repeated blockades. Laws criminalizing roadblocks have been enacted and challenged.
laws.penalty: Organized roadblocks: criminal charges up to 6 years; violence in protest: aggravated penalties; state security forces: accountability mechanisms for excessive force
exceptions: Peaceful protest is constitutionally protected
Traditional indigenous community assemblies are protected
Prior consultation processes are mandatory

quiz.q: What record does Peru hold in Latin America regarding the mining sector?
options: Leads the region in mining-related social conflicts
quiz.explanation: Peru's Ombudsman's office records hundreds of active social conflicts between extractive companies and communities — making Peru the leader in Latin America for mining-related social conflict.

laws.title: Executive Governance Decrees
laws.subtitle: Peru emergency powers and political crisis legal framework
laws.fullDescription: Peru has experienced a prolonged political crisis leading to frequent use of executive emergency decrees. The constitutional framework allows the president to declare states of emergency suspending certain rights, and Congress has the power to remove the president through moral incapacity proceedings. This has resulted in multiple presidential removals and emergency governance periods. Citizens should be aware that political instability can lead to sudden changes in regulations and enforcement priorities.
laws.penalty: Violations of emergency decrees carry fines and potential detention; curfew violations during declared emergencies are strictly enforced
exceptions: Medical emergencies allow curfew violations
Essential services workers exempt from movement restrictions
Diplomatic personnel not subject to emergency restrictions

quiz.q: What constitutional mechanism has been used to remove presidents in Peru's recent political crises?
quiz.explanation: The Peruvian Congress has used moral incapacity proceedings under the constitution to remove presidents during the country's political crises.

laws.title: Mining Community Consultation Requirements
laws.subtitle: Peru's prior consultation law for indigenous and rural communities
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Law of Prior Consultation requires government agencies to conduct good-faith consultations with indigenous communities before approving mining, energy, or infrastructure projects that may affect their territories or way of life, implementing ILO Convention 169. The process must be conducted in indigenous languages, allow sufficient time for deliberation, and genuinely seek consensus rather than just informing communities. Courts have struck down several mining and oil projects for failure to properly consult. The law has been controversial with both industry groups claiming it creates delays and indigenous groups saying it is not fully implemented.
laws.penalty: Projects approved without proper consultation can be challenged in court and suspended; government officials who approve projects without consultation face administrative liability; companies that act on improperly approved projects risk project suspension
exceptions: Projects that do not affect indigenous territorial rights may not require prior consultation
Emergency infrastructure has expedited consultation timelines
Projects with pre-existing community agreements may satisfy consultation requirements
laws.sourceLabel: Peru Ministry of Energy and Mines

quiz.q: What international labor convention does Peru's prior consultation law implement?
options: ILO Convention 87 on Freedom of Association
ILO Convention 169 on Indigenous and Tribal Peoples
quiz.explanation: Peru's prior consultation law implements ILO Convention 169 on Indigenous and Tribal Peoples, which requires states to consult indigenous peoples in good faith before approving projects that may affect their rights and territories.

laws.title: Closed Party List Electoral Reforms
laws.subtitle: Peru's changes to its electoral system and political party laws
laws.fullDescription: Peru has made multiple attempts to reform its fragmented political system, which has seen rapid turnover of presidents and parties due to proportional representation allowing many small parties to win seats. Reforms have included requiring parties to meet minimum vote thresholds to enter congress, restricting party hopping by legislators, requiring more robust party membership lists and primaries, and tightening campaign finance rules. Despite reforms, Peru continues to have significant political fragmentation. Electoral authorities (ONPE and JNE) administer and adjudicate electoral disputes.
laws.penalty: Campaign finance violations carry fines proportional to violation size; party membership fraud carries fines and decertification; electoral fraud carries 4 to 8 years imprisonment
exceptions: Indigenous and Amazonian community representation has protected minimum seats in some regional councils
Alliance parties can combine vote thresholds
Parties with geographic concentration may qualify differently

quiz.q: What electoral system problem has Peru's political reforms been attempting to address?
options: Too few political parties dominating the system
Extreme political fragmentation with many small parties
quiz.explanation: Peru's electoral reforms have targeted extreme political fragmentation — a system where many small parties each win a few congressional seats, making it nearly impossible to form stable governing coalitions and contributing to the pattern of presidential impeachments.

laws.title: Peru Constitutional Crisis and Presidential Impeachment Law
laws.subtitle: Permanent incapacity doctrine enabling presidential removal
laws.fullDescription: Peru's constitution allows Congress to remove a president by declaring 'moral incapacity' under Article 113. This mechanism, originally intended for mental or physical disability, has been broadly interpreted to cover political misconduct. Between 2016 and 2023, three presidents faced impeachment attempts; two were successfully removed. The doctrine has created a pattern of executive instability, with the Constitutional Tribunal ruling in 2023 on the limits of congressional removal power.
laws.penalty: A removed president faces loss of office and five-year ban from public positions. Criminal prosecution is separate and requires lifting of immunity through congressional vote.
exceptions: Vice presidents assume office automatically upon removal
Caretaker government provisions apply if both president and VP are unavailable

quiz.q: Under what constitutional provision can Peru's Congress remove a president?
quiz.explanation: Article 113 of Peru's constitution allows Congress to declare a president's 'moral incapacity,' a provision interpreted broadly to cover political misconduct and used to remove multiple presidents.

laws.title: Peru Mining Conflict and Las Bambas Resolution Efforts
laws.subtitle: Recurring community blockades at major copper mine
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Las Bambas copper mine (operated by MMG, majority-owned by a Chinese consortium) has faced recurring road blockades by indigenous Apurímac communities since 2015. Community protests — over land compensation, water contamination concerns, and unfulfilled infrastructure promises — have periodically halted the mine that produces 1–2% of global copper supply. The Boluarte government negotiated new community benefit agreements in 2023–2024, while enacting changes to Peru's prior consultation process requiring faster environmental hearings.
laws.penalty: Blocking public infrastructure or mining access roads: criminal prosecution under Peru's Penal Code for 'extortion' or 'obstructing infrastructure,' with penalties of 3–6 years imprisonment under emergency decrees.
exceptions: Prior consultation rights of indigenous communities under ILO Convention 169 must be respected before new concession areas
Peaceful protest not involving blockades protected under constitutional freedom of assembly
laws.sourceLabel: Congreso de la República del Perú

quiz.q: What percentage of global copper supply does Peru's Las Bambas mine represent?
quiz.explanation: Peru's Las Bambas copper mine produces approximately 1-2% of the world's copper supply, making it strategically significant for global supply chains — and making the recurring community blockades a major economic concern for Peru and international copper markets.

laws.title: Peru Amazon Protection and Illegal Mining Crackdown
laws.subtitle: La Pampa illegal gold mining eradication and forest protection
laws.fullDescription: Peru achieved significant success in its multi-year operation to eradicate the La Pampa illegal gold mining camp in Madre de Dios — one of Latin America's most destructive mining sites — through Operación Mercurio. The operation, which began in 2019 and continued with periodic reinforcements through 2023–2024, removed thousands of illegal miners from the protected Tambopata Reserve buffer zone, dramatically reducing the area of destroyed forest. Mercury contamination remained a major long-term environmental challenge.
laws.penalty: Illegal gold mining in protected areas: imprisonment of 4–8 years under Peru's Environmental Criminal Code. Mercury use in artisanal gold processing (banned since 2002): fines of up to PEN 500,000 per operation and equipment seizure.
exceptions: Formalized artisanal miners in designated Zones of Informal Mining Formalization (ZOFIMIN) may continue operating while completing legalization process
Indigenous communities mining gold for subsistence on ancestral territories subject to separate consultation and regulation process
laws.sourceLabel: Congreso de la República del Perú

quiz.q: What was the name of Peru's major illegal gold mining operation that Operación Mercurio targeted?
quiz.explanation: La Pampa was the massive illegal gold mining camp in Peru's Madre de Dios region that Operación Mercurio targeted — one of Latin America's most destructive mining sites, where thousands of illegal miners had deforested and contaminated large areas of the Amazonian Tambopata Reserve buffer zone.

laws.title: Mining Conflict Resolution and Comunidades Law
laws.subtitle: New framework for resolving indigenous community mining disputes
laws.fullDescription: Peru enacted legislation strengthening the prior consultation rights of indigenous communities (comunidades campesinas and nativas) before mining projects are approved on or near their lands. The law required companies to negotiate community benefit agreements and created a national register of unresolved mining conflicts with mandatory mediation timelines.
laws.penalty: Mining companies that skip prior consultation face project suspension and fines up to $2M USD
exceptions: Artisanal and small-scale miners with existing community agreements
Exploration permits issued before the law's enactment
laws.sourceLabel: Ministerio de Energía y Minas Perú

quiz.q: What does 'prior consultation' mean in Peru's indigenous mining law?
options: Consulting with the Environment Ministry first
Mandatory negotiation with indigenous communities before project approval
quiz.explanation: Prior consultation (consulta previa) requires companies to negotiate in good faith with affected indigenous communities before a mining project can be approved on or near their lands.

laws.title: Presidential Immunity and Boluarte Corruption Investigations
laws.subtitle: Peru's constitutional immunity provisions and anti-corruption reform
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Congress debated and partially reformed presidential immunity provisions following mass protests over President Boluarte's handling of post-Castillo political crisis. The Constitutional Tribunal ruled on the scope of presidential immunity while multiple Congressional investigations proceeded. Peru's chronic political instability — with six presidents in six years — prompted calls for constitutional reform.
laws.penalty: Presidential immunity does not cover ongoing criminal investigations for crimes committed before or after term; Congress may lift immunity
exceptions: Active impeachment proceedings allow investigation without formal immunity lift
Interpol red notices enforceable regardless of domestic immunity claims
laws.sourceLabel: Congreso de la República del Perú

quiz.q: How many presidents did Peru have in approximately six years leading up to the Boluarte administration?
quiz.explanation: Peru experienced extraordinary political instability with approximately six different presidents in six years, prompting widespread calls for constitutional reform to create more governmental stability.

laws.title: Amazon Protected Areas Expansion
laws.subtitle: Peru significantly expands protected areas in the Amazon
laws.fullDescription: Peru enacted legislation significantly expanding its network of protected areas in the Amazon, creating new national parks and reservas comunales for indigenous communities. The expansion was partly funded through debt-for-nature swaps and international conservation finance. Indigenous territorial rights were strengthened and illegal miners and loggers operating in new protected zones faced enhanced penalties.
laws.penalty: Illegal logging in newly protected areas: up to 10 years imprisonment; illegal gold mining: up to 8 years
exceptions: Pre-existing indigenous communities within newly designated parks retain territorial rights
Scientific research under SERNANP permit exempt from access restrictions
laws.sourceLabel: Congreso de la República del Perú

quiz.q: What financial mechanism did Peru use to fund Amazon protected area expansion?
quiz.explanation: Peru used debt-for-nature swaps — where portions of national debt are forgiven in exchange for conservation commitments — and international conservation finance to fund the expansion of its Amazon protected area network.

laws.title: Peruvian Mining Investment Revival and Conflict Resolution
laws.subtitle: Peru streamlines mining approvals while improving community consultation
laws.fullDescription: Peru enacted legislation reviving stalled mining investment by streamlining environmental impact assessments, creating faster dispute resolution mechanisms for community conflicts, and establishing a prior consultation registry. Peru targeted $60 billion in mining investment, with major copper projects (Quellaveco, Tía María) and lithium exploration underway.
laws.penalty: Mining companies that bypass updated consultation requirements: project suspension; community leaders who incite violence against legally approved mines: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Small-scale mining operations under 350 hectares use simplified EIA procedures
Artisanal mining formalisation programmes have separate compliance pathways
laws.sourceLabel: Congreso de la República del Perú

quiz.q: What total mining investment value is Peru targeting?
quiz.explanation: Peru has set a target of attracting $60 billion in mining investment — leveraging its world-class copper, lithium, and precious metal deposits — as a cornerstone of the country's economic development strategy.

laws.title: Peru Critical Minerals Priority Development Act
laws.subtitle: Fast-tracking copper, lithium and rare earth projects
laws.fullDescription: Peru enacted the Critical Minerals Priority Development Act 2025, designating copper, lithium, zinc, silver, and molybdenum projects as national strategic priorities. The law establishes a 180-day maximum permitting timeline for designated projects (versus the previous 4-7 year average), creates a Special Commission for Conflict Prevention in Mining Communities with binding mediation authority, requires prior consultation with indigenous communities within 90 days of project announcement, and introduces community benefit agreements mandating 5% of project value investment in local infrastructure. The law followed years of project delays due to social conflicts that cost Peru billions in stalled investment.
laws.penalty: Mining without prior consultation completion: project suspension plus $10 million fine; failure to fund community benefit agreement: license revocation; illegal mining: 8-15 years imprisonment
exceptions: Artisanal mining formalization process provides amnesty pathway for informal operators
Environmental emergency response activities exempt from standard permitting timelines
Exploration licenses under 500 hectares have simplified permitting
laws.sourceLabel: Peru Ministry of Energy and Mines

quiz.q: What maximum permitting timeline did Peru's Critical Minerals Priority Development Act establish for designated strategic mineral projects?
quiz.explanation: Peru's Critical Minerals Priority Development Act set a 180-day maximum permitting timeline for designated strategic projects, dramatically reducing the previous average of 4-7 years.

laws.title: Peru Political Fragmentation and Anti-Corruption Governance
laws.subtitle: Strengthening institutions amid instability
laws.fullDescription: Peru enacted the Democratic Governance and Anti-Corruption Strengthening Act 2025 following years of extraordinary political instability (six presidents in six years between 2018-2024). The law strengthens the Contraloría General with enhanced audit powers and criminal referral authority, establishes the National Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office as independent entity outside Ministry of Justice control, introduces constitutional amendments requiring 2/3 congressional majority to remove presidents except for incapacitation or conviction (closing the 'moral incapacitation' loophole that enabled removals), mandates political party organizational minimums preventing one-person 'party-vehicles,' and creates the Peru Democratic Stability Fund providing institutional continuity resources during government transitions.
laws.penalty: Anti-Corruption Prosecutor obstruction: 20 years imprisonment; political party registration fraud: permanent disqualification; Democratic Stability Fund misuse: 25 years imprisonment plus personal liability
exceptions: Genuine impeachment for criminal conviction retains simple majority requirement
Emergency powers during natural disasters not subject to new removal provisions
Regional and local governments have modified accountability framework

quiz.q: Approximately how many presidents did Peru have in the six years between 2018-2024?
quiz.explanation: Peru experienced extraordinary political instability with approximately six presidents between 2018-2024 — a revolving door of leadership including Pedro Castillo's removal for attempted coup, creating the governance crisis the 2025 Democratic Governance Act addresses.

laws.title: Peru Amazon Permanent Protection and Deforestation Zero Law
laws.subtitle: Protecting remaining Amazonian primary forest
laws.fullDescription: Peru enacted the Amazon Permanent Protection and Zero Deforestation Act 2025, responding to accelerating deforestation driven by illegal gold mining, coca cultivation, and oil palm expansion. The law designates all remaining primary Amazon forest in Peru as permanently protected regardless of ownership status, requires prior consultation with indigenous communities for any development affecting Amazon watersheds, creates the Amazon Forest Guard Force deploying 5,000 trained forest rangers including indigenous community members, introduces satellite monitoring with 48-hour enforcement response protocols, establishes a Forest Carbon Revenue Fund distributing international carbon payments directly to indigenous territories, and criminalizes deforestation funding as an environmental crime equivalent to money laundering.
laws.penalty: Primary forest clearing above 0.5 hectares: 25 years imprisonment; deforestation financing: 20 years plus unlimited asset forfeiture; forest guard assault: 30 years; gold mining in protected watersheds: life imprisonment
exceptions: Indigenous communities' traditional land management including controlled clearing protected under ILO 169
Emergency natural disaster response may require limited vegetation clearing with SERNANP authorization
Scientific research corridors with minimal impact have expedited authorization

quiz.q: What three major drivers of Amazon deforestation does Peru's 2025 Zero Deforestation Act specifically target?
options: Illegal gold mining, coca cultivation, and oil palm
quiz.explanation: Peru's Amazon Permanent Protection Act specifically targets illegal gold mining, coca cultivation, and oil palm expansion as the three major current drivers of Amazon deforestation in Peru — each requiring different enforcement and alternative livelihood strategies.

laws.title: Boluarte Governability and Political Crisis Management Act
laws.subtitle: Governance amid ongoing legitimacy challenges
laws.fullDescription: Peru's President Boluarte, who came to power following Pedro Castillo's failed self-coup, enacted legislation aimed at stabilizing governance amid persistent protests from southern regions and attempts by Congress to limit judicial oversight of politicians. The law restructures the attorney general's office, addresses demands from the agricultural and mining sectors, and establishes new mechanisms for regional development funding aimed at appeasing highland communities that have continued protests demanding early elections.
laws.penalty: Protest organizers who block critical infrastructure (mines, highways, airports) face up to eight years imprisonment. Officials who use excessive force against protesters face criminal charges.
exceptions: Legitimate labor strikes with prior notice retain full protection
Indigenous communities exercising consultation rights cannot be charged for peaceful assembly near project sites

quiz.q: How did President Boluarte come to power in Peru?
options: Succeeded Pedro Castillo who was impeached after a failed self-coup
Won a runoff election against Keiko Fujimori
quiz.explanation: Dina Boluarte was vice president and became president when Pedro Castillo was impeached and arrested after attempting to dissolve Congress and rule by decree in December 2022 — a self-coup that backfired within hours.

laws.title: Mining Conflict Resolution and Community Consent Act
laws.subtitle: Addressing Peru's chronic anti-mining protests
laws.fullDescription: Peru enacted legislation creating structured frameworks for resolving conflicts between mining companies and communities. The law mandates early, genuine consultation with affected communities before major mining projects begin, creates a national conflict resolution authority, establishes minimum community benefit requirements from mine revenues, and creates environmental restoration bonds that companies must fund upfront.
laws.penalty: Mining companies that begin operations without completing community consultation face project suspension. Companies that fail to maintain environmental restoration bonds face license revocation.
exceptions: Artisanal and small-scale mining in traditionally-mined areas has a simplified consultation process
Emergency mining operations needed for critical mineral supply chains during declared national security situations receive expedited review

quiz.q: What type of protests have been chronically disrupting Peru's mining industry, making it one of the world's most conflict-prone mining countries?
options: Environmental anti-mining community protests blocking operations
quiz.explanation: Peru is one of the world's most conflict-prone mining countries, with frequent community protests blocking operations at major copper, gold, and silver mines. Communities often feel they receive insufficient benefits from mine revenues while bearing environmental costs.

laws.title: Machu Picchu Sustainable Tourism and Inca Heritage Act
laws.subtitle: Protecting UNESCO site from over-tourism
laws.fullDescription: Peru enacted comprehensive Machu Picchu management legislation following visitor surge damage and UNESCO threats to list the site as World Heritage in Danger. The law reduces maximum daily visitors from 4,500 to 3,000, requires timed entry tickets booked weeks in advance, bans single-use plastics on the site, creates stricter trail management for the Inca Trail, funds restoration of deteriorating stone structures, and creates a community benefit fund for nearby Aguas Calientes.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized entry to restricted areas of Machu Picchu carries fines up to USD 4,000 and immediate removal. Guides who bring unauthorized visitors face permanent license revocation.
exceptions: Scientific and archaeological researchers retain access outside tourist hours with special permits
Peruvian citizens receive a significantly reduced admission price with a separate allocation of daily tickets

quiz.q: What Andean mountain does Machu Picchu sit on, giving the site its name?
quiz.explanation: Machu Picchu sits on the mountain of the same name. In Quechua, 'Machu Picchu' means 'Old Mountain.' The neighboring peak Huayna Picchu ('Young Mountain') overlooks the citadel and is itself a popular (and limited) hiking destination.

laws.title: Peru Congressional Immunity Reform and Anti-Corruption Act
laws.subtitle: Legislative Accountability and Corruption Prevention Law
laws.fullDescription: Limits parliamentary immunity to legislative acts only, stripping protection for criminal acts committed before or during congressional service. The law responds to widespread public anger over corruption scandals involving legislators. It establishes an independent anti-corruption prosecutor with congressional oversight authority, mandates asset declarations for all congressional candidates, and creates recall mechanisms for legislators convicted of crimes.
laws.penalty: Automatic legislative expulsion for conviction of corruption or serious crimes; criminal prosecution without immunity
exceptions: Purely legislative acts and votes remain immune from prosecution
Political speech in Congress retains full protection

quiz.q: What does Peru's Congressional Immunity Reform Act limit immunity to?
quiz.explanation: Peru's reform limits congressional immunity to legislative acts only, stripping protection for criminal acts before or during service.

laws.title: Peru Las Bambas Copper Mine and Community Conflict Resolution Act
laws.subtitle: Mining Social License and Indigenous Consultation Law
laws.fullDescription: Addresses recurring blockades of Peru's Las Bambas copper mine by local Apurímac communities over land use and environmental concerns. The law creates permanent consultation and compensation mechanisms for communities affected by major mines, establishes community dividend rights from mine revenues, mandates environmental monitoring with community participation, and creates binding dispute resolution for mining-community conflicts.
laws.penalty: Administrative sanctions for mining companies failing consultation requirements; court injunctions for blockade-organizers causing economic damage
exceptions: Emergency mine operations to prevent environmental damage may continue during disputes
Pre-existing community agreements honored during transition

quiz.q: In which Peruvian region is the Las Bambas copper mine located?
quiz.explanation: Las Bambas copper mine is located in Peru's Apurímac region, where local communities have staged recurring blockades over land and environmental concerns.

laws.title: Peru Boluarte Government Protests and Police Use of Force Act
laws.subtitle: Civil Unrest Response and Accountability Law
laws.fullDescription: Addresses the legal aftermath of security force actions during the 2022-2023 protests following Castillo's removal that killed nearly 60 protesters. The law creates a truth commission for protest deaths, establishes police use of force guidelines, creates accountability mechanisms for security forces, provides reparations for victims' families, and creates transparency requirements for security force operations during civil unrest.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for security force members who used disproportionate force; prison sentences for orders to fire on protesters
exceptions: Legitimate self-defense in response to armed attack
Emergency security operations facing imminent lethal threat

quiz.q: Approximately how many protesters were killed during Peru's 2022-2023 civil unrest?
quiz.explanation: Nearly 60 protesters were killed during Peru's 2022-2023 civil unrest following President Castillo's removal, driving accountability reforms.

laws.title: Peru Amazon Illegal Gold Mining and MAPE Regulation Act
laws.subtitle: Artisanal Mining Formalization and Mercury Ban Law
laws.fullDescription: Addresses Peru's serious problem of illegal and informal artisanal gold mining (MAPE) in the Amazon, particularly in Madre de Dios region. The law creates the MAPE Formalization Registry with clear paths to legal status, mandates mercury-free mining techniques, creates military deployment to illegal mining zones, establishes mercury trade controls, and creates income alternatives for former illegal miners.
laws.penalty: Criminal prosecution for mercury use in artisanal mining; up to 6 years for illegal mining in protected areas
exceptions: Formalized miners with environmental management plans operate legally
Traditional communities with ancestral mining practices have modified requirements
laws.sourceLabel: Peru Ministry of Energy and Mines

quiz.q: In which Peruvian Amazon region is illegal artisanal gold mining most concentrated?
quiz.explanation: Peru's illegal artisanal gold mining problem is most concentrated in Madre de Dios, which has experienced severe deforestation and mercury contamination.

laws.title: Congress-Judiciary Conflict and Impeachment Crisis
laws.subtitle: Peru's Chronic Institutional Dysfunction
laws.fullDescription: Peru continued its pattern of institutional instability with Congress passing laws to protect politicians from prosecution, weaken the attorney general's office, and restrict international court jurisdiction. The country had five presidents in just a few years. Anti-democratic backsliding prompted citizen protests but Congress maintained its grip on judicial reform.
laws.penalty: No direct penalties; rule of law erosion has indirect consequences
exceptions: Constitutional Court partial oversight
Inter-American Court of Human Rights jurisdiction

quiz.q: Approximately how many presidents did Peru have between 2016 and 2024?
quiz.explanation: Peru had approximately five presidents between 2016 and 2024 due to impeachments, resignations, and institutional crises reflecting chronic political dysfunction.

laws.title: Las Bambas and Mining Conflict Management
laws.subtitle: Community Protests Disrupt Copper Supply
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Las Bambas copper mine, one of the world's largest, faced repeated blockades by local indigenous communities demanding better benefit-sharing and environmental mitigation. The mine had faced over 1,000 days of blockades since opening. The government mediated but underlying community grievances remained unresolved.
laws.penalty: Criminal charges for blockade organizers; police enforcement
exceptions: Community consultation rights under ILO 169
Negotiated access corridor agreements

quiz.q: What type of resource is Las Bambas in Peru known for?
