quiz.explanation: Las Bambas is one of the world's largest copper mines, making community conflicts over its operation a major issue for global copper supply.

laws.title: Anti-Corruption Congress Laws and Immunity
laws.subtitle: Peru Congress Shields Members From Prosecution
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Congress passed legislation that critics argued was designed to protect its members from corruption prosecution, including laws restricting attorney general powers, extending statutes of limitations, and creating special immunity provisions. Civil society and prosecutors organized resistance while Peru faced criticism from the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties for legislation; prosecutorial restrictions
exceptions: Constitutional court review
Inter-American human rights system

quiz.q: What did Peru's Congress pass that was criticized as protecting legislators from prosecution?
options: Laws restricting attorney general powers and creating immunity provisions
quiz.explanation: Peru's Congress passed laws restricting the attorney general's powers and creating special immunity provisions, widely criticized as designed to protect legislators from corruption prosecution.

laws.title: Amazon Deforestation and Community Forestry
laws.subtitle: Peru Recognizes Indigenous Territorial Rights
laws.fullDescription: Peru registered millions of hectares of indigenous territorial rights in the Amazon, a landmark step in protecting forest and indigenous communities. The titling process accelerated under international pressure and climate finance commitments. However, illegal mining, logging, and coca cultivation continued threatening registered territories.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for illegal activities in titled indigenous territories
exceptions: Subsistence activities on traditional lands
Government project consultation rights

quiz.q: What did Peru register to help protect the Amazon and indigenous communities?
options: Indigenous territorial rights for millions of hectares
quiz.explanation: Peru registered millions of hectares of indigenous territorial rights, providing legal protection for both indigenous communities and the Amazon forests they inhabit.

laws.title: Anchovy Fishery and Fishmeal Industry
laws.subtitle: Peru Leads Global Fishmeal Production
laws.fullDescription: Peru is the world's largest fishmeal and fish oil producer, based on its massive anchovy fishery in the Humboldt Current. The industry provides proteins for global aquaculture and livestock. El Nino disruptions periodically collapse anchovy stocks. Peru balanced fishing quotas against sustainability concerns and export revenues.
laws.penalty: Criminal penalties for illegal fishing; quota violations
exceptions: Traditional artisanal fishing exemptions
Scientific fishing permits

quiz.q: What current makes Peru's fishery the world's most productive?
quiz.explanation: The Humboldt Current brings cold, nutrient-rich water to Peru's coast, creating extraordinarily productive fishing grounds for anchovy and other species.

laws.title: Political Instability and Presidential Impeachments
laws.subtitle: Peru cycles through presidents amid chronic institutional crisis
laws.fullDescription: Peru has had five presidents in five years, with political instability becoming the norm. Pedro Castillo attempted a coup, was arrested, and imprisoned. Dina Boluarte took over amid deadly protests. Congress and the executive branch are in constant conflict. The prosecutor's office investigates presidents and Congress members. Despite this political chaos, Peru's economy (driven by copper, gold, and agriculture) has remained relatively stable. The disconnect between political dysfunction and economic resilience is a defining feature.
laws.penalty: Congressional impeachment requires 87 votes out of 130 for 'moral incapacity' removal of presidents
exceptions: Sitting presidents maintain immunity from prosecution while in office
Former presidents can be prosecuted after leaving office, as multiple have been

laws.title: Tía María Mine Conflict and Social License Crisis
laws.subtitle: Peru's copper mine struggles to gain community acceptance
laws.fullDescription: Peru has some of the world's largest copper reserves but faces repeated conflicts between mining companies and local communities over water, land, and environmental impacts. The Tía María copper project has been blocked for over a decade by community opposition despite permits. Las Bambas copper mine faces regular roadblocks. Peru's mining conflicts cost billions in lost production. The concept of 'social license to operate' — community acceptance beyond legal permits — has become central to mining strategy globally.
laws.penalty: Mining operations without social license face community blockades and government suspension of activities
exceptions: National strategic mining projects can invoke emergency operating provisions
Environmental monitoring and remediation activities continue during conflicts to protect existing impacts

laws.title: Gastronomy Tourism and Culinary Soft Power
laws.subtitle: Peru's cuisine becomes global phenomenon driving tourism
laws.fullDescription: Peru's gastronomy — ceviche, lomo saltado, causa, tiradito — has become a global phenomenon. Nobu, Maido, and Central (rated #1 in the world) are among the world's top restaurants. Lima is considered one of the world's top food cities. Gastronomic tourism drives billions in revenue. Peru's biodiversity (potato origin center with 4,000 varieties, 3,000 types of chili peppers) provides unique ingredients. The culinary boom creates direct economic benefits for farmers and indirect benefits through tourism.
laws.penalty: Geographic indication protections for Peruvian pisco, ají amarillo, and other products require compliance for use abroad
exceptions: Home cooks and traditional preparation exempt from commercial food safety requirements
Cultural gastronomy events and festivals have simplified health and safety compliance

quiz.q: How many potato varieties originate from Peru?
quiz.explanation: Peru is the origin center of potatoes with approximately 4,000 varieties — from purple to yellow to freeze-dried chuño — making Peru's Andes the world's most important repository of potato genetic diversity.

laws.title: Political Instability and Boluarte Legitimacy Crisis
laws.subtitle: Peru's cycle of presidential crises and congressional conflicts
laws.fullDescription: Peru has experienced extraordinary political instability, with six presidents in seven years (2016-2023). The removal and imprisonment of Pedro Castillo — elected as a leftist rural teacher in 2021 — after his self-coup attempt in December 2022 (trying to dissolve Congress before impeachment) brought Dina Boluarte to power as the first female president. Post-Castillo protests demanding her resignation and new elections resulted in over 60 deaths in police-civilian clashes. Boluarte has been investigated for allegedly being slow to respond to the protests and for various corruption allegations. Peru's political system features a congress that has repeatedly used impeachment ('vacancia') against executives and executives that have governed by decree. Underlying the political chaos are deep social divisions between coastal urban elites and rural indigenous populations who feel excluded from economic governance. Peru has significant natural resources (copper, gold, silver, lithium) but widespread rural poverty.
laws.penalty: Political crimes including self-coup attempts carry criminal prosecution; anti-protest laws have been used against demonstrators
exceptions: Indigenous consultation rights under ILO Convention 169 provide some protections for resource development on traditional lands

quiz.q: What did Pedro Castillo attempt in December 2022 that led to his removal from office?
options: He attempted to cancel upcoming elections
He tried to dissolve Congress before it could impeach him
He declared martial law and arrested opposition leaders
He attempted to hold an unauthorized constitutional referendum
quiz.explanation: Pedro Castillo attempted a self-coup by trying to dissolve Congress before it could vote on his impeachment — a move Congress declared unconstitutional. Castillo was instead arrested, and Vice President Dina Boluarte became president.

laws.title: Mining Conflict and Community Opposition to Resource Extraction
laws.subtitle: Peru's copper wealth facing sustained social opposition
laws.fullDescription: Peru is one of the world's largest producers of copper, silver, zinc, and gold, with mining representing approximately 15% of GDP and 60% of export revenues. However, Peru faces persistent social conflicts at mining sites, with local communities opposing projects over concerns about water contamination, land rights, and distribution of benefits. The Las Bambas copper mine — one of the world's largest — has faced repeated blockades disrupting operations, with Apurimac communities demanding greater benefits and protecting water sources. The Conga gold-copper project in Cajamarca was effectively stopped by sustained social opposition. Peru's challenge is managing competing interests: national economic interest in mining revenues, local communities bearing environmental and social costs, and the global demand for critical minerals needed for the energy transition. The government has attempted various social dialogue mechanisms with limited success.
laws.penalty: Illegal blockades of mining operations carry criminal penalties; mining companies must comply with environmental and social management plans
exceptions: Indigenous consultation requirements under ILO Convention 169 apply to projects affecting indigenous territories
laws.sourceLabel: Peru Ministry of Energy and Mines

quiz.q: What is the approximate percentage of Peru's export revenues that come from mining?
quiz.explanation: Mining represents approximately 60% of Peru's export revenues, making it critically important to the national economy while also creating persistent social conflicts with communities near mining operations.

laws.title: Presidential Impeachment Culture
laws.subtitle: Peru's revolving door of presidents and political crises
laws.fullDescription: Peru has impeached or removed five presidents in less than a decade, including Pedro Castillo who attempted a coup in December 2022 before being arrested. The country's political instability stems from a fragmented Congress, weak party system and profound urban-rural divides. President Dina Boluarte took office after Castillo's arrest amid deadly protests that killed dozens. Political gridlock has hampered economic policy and infrastructure development.
laws.penalty: Impeachment requires Congressional supermajority; removed presidents face criminal prosecution in many cases
exceptions: Presidential immunity applies during term for official acts
Constitutional court can review impeachment proceedings

quiz.q: How many Peruvian presidents have been impeached or removed in the past decade?
quiz.explanation: Peru has impeached or removed five presidents in less than a decade, reflecting profound political instability and a dysfunctional relationship between executive and legislative branches.

laws.title: Illegal Gold Mining Amazon Devastation
laws.subtitle: Peru battles illegal miners destroying Amazon with mercury
laws.fullDescription: Illegal gold mining, known as minería ilegal, has devastated sections of the Peruvian Amazon, particularly in the Madre de Dios region. Miners use mercury to process gold, poisoning rivers and the Indigenous communities that depend on them. Satellite imagery shows vast tracts of former jungle converted to barren moonscapes. Military and police operations have made repeated attempts to expel miners but face massive economic incentives that attract tens of thousands of miners. The illegal economy generates billions and funds corruption throughout the supply chain.
laws.penalty: Illegal mining criminalized with prison terms; mining equipment seized and destroyed by security forces
exceptions: Small-scale artisanal mining with permits allowed in designated areas
Indigenous community members have different legal treatment for subsistence mining
laws.sourceLabel: Peruvian Ministry of Energy and Mines

quiz.q: What chemical do illegal gold miners use to process gold that poisons Amazonian rivers?
quiz.explanation: Illegal gold miners use mercury to process gold ore, and the mercury contamination poisons rivers and fish—critically threatening the health of Indigenous communities in the Peruvian Amazon who depend on these waterways for food and water.

laws.title: Machu Picchu Tech Tourism Platform
laws.subtitle: Peru digitizes ancient heritage and modernizes tourist management
laws.fullDescription: Peru has implemented digital ticketing and time-slot management for Machu Picchu, limiting daily visitors to protect the World Heritage Site. The system requires advance online booking, eliminating the spontaneous visit experience but protecting the site from overuse. Digital platforms have transformed how Peru's tourism industry operates. The government's digitization of heritage site access represents a broader effort to modernize government services. Peru's technology sector is growing with Limeño startups emerging in fintech and agtech.
laws.penalty: Entering Machu Picchu without valid digital ticket subject to removal from site; ticket scalping criminally prosecuted
exceptions: Local Cusco residents have different access procedures
Accredited researchers have special access beyond tourist quotas

quiz.q: What system has Peru implemented to protect Machu Picchu from over-tourism?
options: Digital ticketing with advance online booking and time slots
quiz.explanation: Peru implemented digital ticketing with advance online booking and time slots for Machu Picchu, limiting daily visitors and eliminating spontaneous visits to protect the World Heritage Site from the damage caused by overtourism.

laws.title: Mining Revenue and Community Conflicts
laws.subtitle: Peru's copper wealth triggers local protests blocking production
laws.fullDescription: Peru is the world's second largest copper producer and significant gold and silver producer. However mining projects frequently face protests from local communities citing environmental damage, water contamination and insufficient revenue sharing. The Las Bambas mine has been blockaded dozens of times. The Conga project was cancelled after years of protests. Community conflicts have cost billions in lost production. The Boluarte government has declared states of emergency in mining areas to guarantee operations while community grievances remain unresolved.
laws.penalty: Mining companies must obtain social license through community consultation; prior consultation required for projects affecting indigenous communities
exceptions: National security declarations allow mine operations during blockades
State arbitration mechanisms exist for community compensation disputes
laws.sourceLabel: Peruvian Ministry of Energy and Mines

quiz.q: What is Peru's ranking in global copper production?
quiz.explanation: Peru is the world's second largest copper producer (after Chile), with abundant silver and gold also produced—but mining revenues frequently trigger community protests over environmental damage, water impacts and insufficient local benefit sharing.

laws.title: Environmental Framework Law and Nationally Determined Contributions
laws.subtitle: Protecting the Amazon and Andes
laws.fullDescription: Peru's General Environmental Law (Law 28,611) and subsequent climate commitments set a target to reduce 30% of projected emissions by 2030. Peru is one of the ten most biodiverse countries on Earth, with Amazon rainforest, Andean highlands, and coastal desert. The country has a severe deforestation problem, with illegal gold mining and coca cultivation driving Amazon destruction. Peru's NDC also includes adaptation measures for glacier retreat — the Andes glaciers supply water to millions — and coastal flooding from El Niño intensification.
laws.penalty: Environmental fines ranging from 0.1 to 30,000 UIT (tax units); permit revocation; criminal charges for serious violations
exceptions: Indigenous community traditional activities
Subsistence farming

laws.title: Peru Universal Health Insurance Law
laws.subtitle: SIS for the Poor, EsSalud for Workers
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Universal Health Insurance Law (Law 29344, 2009) created a framework for universal health coverage through three mechanisms: SIS (Integral Health Insurance) for the poor, EsSalud for formal workers, and private insurance for those who can afford it. Despite the framework, Peru's health system remains underfunded — the COVID-19 pandemic revealed severe weaknesses when Peru had the world's highest per-capita COVID death rate. Peru's community health worker (promotor de salud) program reaches remote Andean and Amazonian communities. Malnutrition in indigenous children remains a major challenge.
laws.penalty: Employers must enroll workers in EsSalud; criminal penalties for non-enrollment; SIS coverage is a right that can be demanded
exceptions: Self-employed and informal workers can voluntarily affiliate to SIS
Remote communities may use alternative care models

laws.title: Peru Labor Rights and Informal Economy
laws.subtitle: CTS and the Formal-Informal Divide
laws.fullDescription: Peru's labor code provides workers with significant protections in the formal sector: CTS (Compensation for Time of Service) — mandatory monthly deposits of half a salary equivalent into a worker's account for use upon job loss; profit sharing in companies with 20+ workers; and extensive health and pension contributions. However, 70%+ of Peruvian workers are in the informal economy, outside these protections. Attempts to formalize the economy through 'special regimes' for small businesses have been controversial. Peru's agricultural workers gained some formalization through the Agrarian Labor Law after major farm worker strikes in 2020.
laws.penalty: CTS non-deposit: judicial recovery with interest; formal sector violations: Ministry of Labor enforcement; labor court system active
exceptions: SME special regime with reduced costs
Domestic workers have adapted protections under Law 27986

laws.title: Peru University Reform Law
laws.subtitle: Accreditation and Quality Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Peru's University Law 30220 (2014) created SUNEDU (National Superintendency of Higher Education) to establish mandatory licensing and quality standards for Peru's universities — many of which had extremely low standards. The reform was transformative: SUNEDU denied licenses to 48 universities (mostly private) that could not meet basic quality standards, affecting 150,000 students who had to transfer. Peru's public universities are free for students who pass entrance exams. Massive student protests have demanded quality education. Peru also has significant non-formal education challenges in rural, indigenous, and Amazonian communities.
laws.penalty: Universities without SUNEDU license cannot issue degrees; illegal operation: fines and closure; degree fraud: criminal liability
exceptions: Religious universities under concordat provisions
Military and police academies under separate oversight

laws.title: Migration Law and Venezuelan Integration
laws.subtitle: Peru's immigration management amid regional crisis
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Decree Legislative 1350 (2017) modernized immigration law. Peru hosts over 1.5 million Venezuelan migrants, the third-largest Venezuelan diaspora globally. Peru initially issued humanitarian residency permits to Venezuelans but later tightened requirements, requiring passports (which many Venezuelans cannot obtain from the Maduro government) and visas. Border processing centers have struggled with overwhelming numbers. Peru also has significant Japanese-Peruvian and Chinese-Peruvian communities with historical immigration roots.
laws.penalty: Irregular migrants may be detained and deported; coyotes and human smugglers face 6-12 year imprisonment; exploitation of migrant workers violates labor law
exceptions: Venezuela crisis temporary protection measures have been extended and modified multiple times
MERCOSUR associate member status provides some facilitated entry for member-country nationals

quiz.q: Peru hosts approximately how many Venezuelan migrants, making it one of the largest Venezuelan diaspora communities?
quiz.explanation: Peru hosts approximately 1.5 million Venezuelan migrants, the third-largest Venezuelan diaspora after Colombia and the United States, creating significant integration challenges and periodic policy shifts between welcoming and restrictive approaches.

laws.title: Drug Law and Coca Leaf Heritage
laws.subtitle: Peru's coca cultivation, trafficking, and decriminalization
laws.fullDescription: Peru is the world's second-largest cocaine producer (after Colombia). Coca leaf has deep cultural and traditional significance to Andean peoples — it's legal to grow, sell, and consume coca leaves (but not process into cocaine). Peru's drug law decriminalizes personal possession of small amounts but trafficking carries 15-35 years. The VRAEM (Vraem River Valley) is the world's most concentrated cocaine production zone. Peru has struggled with corruption of police and military by drug trafficking organizations. Under Boluarte's government, counter-narcotics operations intensified.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking: 15-25 years; large-scale trafficking: 25-35 years; personal possession (small amounts): decriminalized; coca leaf possession and consumption: legal; cocaine production: 10-25 years
exceptions: Coca leaf cultivation, sale, and consumption is legal (traditional use)
Personal amounts of cocaine decriminalized (legal gray area)
DEVIDA (anti-drug agency) runs coca crop substitution programs
laws.sourceLabel: Peru Drug Code and DEVIDA Strategy

quiz.q: In Peru, what is the legal status of coca leaf (as opposed to processed cocaine)?
options: Legal to grow, sell, and consume as a traditional product
quiz.explanation: Coca leaf is legal in Peru — it can be grown, sold in markets, and consumed (chewed, made into tea) as it has been for thousands of years in Andean culture. Only the chemical processing of coca leaf into cocaine is illegal.

laws.title: Limited LGBTQ+ Rights and Same-Sex Marriage Debate
laws.subtitle: Peru's conservative stance on LGBTQ+ rights
laws.fullDescription: Peru has limited LGBTQ+ legal protections. Peru does not recognize same-sex marriage or civil unions at the national level. A 2023 Constitutional Tribunal ruling declined to recognize same-sex marriages performed abroad. Peru classified transgender identities as 'mental disorder' under health regulations (decree repealed after pressure). LGBTQ+ individuals face discrimination and violence, including police abuse. Some cities (Lima, Cusco) have local non-discrimination ordinances. Peru's conservative political environment, influenced by the Catholic Church and evangelical groups, has blocked national LGBTQ+ protections.
laws.penalty: No comprehensive LGBTQ+ anti-discrimination law exists nationally; LGBTQ+ individuals may report crimes under general anti-discrimination provisions; hate crimes laws are limited
exceptions: Local ordinances in some cities provide anti-discrimination protections
Federal workers have some protections under general civil service rules
Constitutional protections for equal treatment may be applied in some cases
laws.sourceLabel: Peru MIMP LGBTQ+ Policy and Protections

quiz.q: Peru's Ministry of Health classified transgender identities as what until the classification was challenged and repealed?
quiz.explanation: Peru's Ministry of Health maintained transgender identities in its classification of 'mental disorders' in national health regulations until LGBT rights organizations successfully challenged the classification and it was eventually repealed following international pressure and domestic advocacy.

laws.title: Press Freedom Under Political Instability
laws.subtitle: Peru's turbulent politics and regional violence create significant press freedom challenges
laws.fullDescription: Peru's constitution protects freedom of expression and press (Article 2 No. 4). However, Peru has experienced extreme political instability with multiple presidents and corruption scandals. Journalists covering corruption, mining conflicts, and coca cultivation face threats from criminal organizations and government pressure. Local journalists in the Amazon region and mining areas face particular danger. The Committee to Protect Journalists and RSF regularly document violations. Digital surveillance of journalists is a growing concern. State advertising is used as a mechanism to reward or punish media outlets.
laws.penalty: Criminal defamation laws can be used against journalists; harassment and threats are common especially in conflict areas
exceptions: Federal constitutional protection applies but enforcement varies by region

quiz.q: What mechanism does the Peruvian government use to reward or punish media outlets beyond legal tools?
quiz.explanation: State advertising is used in Peru as a soft power mechanism to reward favorable media coverage and punish critical reporting, with government entities directing advertising budgets toward supportive outlets and withholding from critical ones.

laws.title: Personal Data Protection Law and Platform Liability Debates
laws.subtitle: Peru has data protection legislation but struggles with online misinformation and platform enforcement
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Personal Data Protection Law (Law 29733, 2011) governs the processing of personal data. The National Authority for Personal Data Protection (ANPD Peru) enforces data rights. Peru has been grappling with social media misinformation, particularly around elections, and has had debates about platform accountability. Political instability has affected digital policy coherence. Peru's government has used social media extensively for communications, and social media has played a significant role in political mobilization. Content moderation on platforms faces challenges in addressing election-related misinformation in Peru's fragmented political landscape.
laws.penalty: Data protection violations: fines up to 100 UIT; ANPD enforcement authority
exceptions: Journalism and academic research exemptions apply

quiz.q: What particular challenge has Peru faced with social media platforms related to its political environment?
options: Social media used for drug trafficking coordination
Addressing election-related misinformation in a fragmented political landscape
Platform refusals to operate in Peru
quiz.explanation: Peru's fragmented political landscape — with numerous small parties and frequent political crises — has made managing election-related misinformation on social media particularly challenging, with platforms struggling to enforce policies consistently across an unusually complex political information environment.

laws.title: SBS Financial Regulation and Financial Inclusion
laws.subtitle: Peru has a comprehensive financial regulator and has made progress in financial inclusion
laws.fullDescription: Peru's financial system is overseen by the Superintendencia de Banca, Seguros y AFP (SBS). Peru has made significant progress in financial inclusion through digital banking — Yape (BCP's app) and Plin have become major digital payment platforms. Peru launched Bim, a mobile money system for the unbanked. Peru's central bank (BCRP) has explored digital currency options. Peru faces challenges with informal economy money flows and some cartel-related AML issues in coca-growing regions. Peru's financial sector includes strong presence of microfinance institutions (cajas municipales) serving rural and low-income populations.
laws.penalty: SBS regulatory enforcement; AML violations subject to criminal prosecution; digital service licensing requirements
exceptions: Microfinance institutions (cajas) have differentiated regulatory requirements

quiz.q: What Peruvian digital payment application became one of Latin America's most-used mobile payment platforms?
quiz.explanation: Yape, launched by Banco de Crédito del Perú (BCP), became one of Latin America's most successful mobile payment apps — reaching tens of millions of users and transforming everyday payments in Peru, alongside competitor Plin, dramatically accelerating digital financial inclusion.

laws.title: Peruvian Law 30021 & Octagonal Food Warning Labels
laws.subtitle: Peru implemented front-of-pack octagonal warnings following Chile's pioneering model
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Law 30021 (Law for the Promotion of Healthy Eating for Children and Adolescents) and its regulations implement front-of-package octagonal warning labels for processed foods and beverages exceeding nutritional thresholds for sodium, sugar, saturated fat, and trans fat. DIGESA (Directorate General of Environmental Health) under the Ministry of Health (MINSA) oversees food safety for human consumption, while SENASA handles animal-origin food safety. Peru is one of the world's greatest centers of food biodiversity — home to over 3,000 potato varieties, hundreds of corn cultivars, and unique Amazonian foods. Peru's food safety system must balance modern commercial standards with preservation of traditional and indigenous food knowledge.
laws.penalty: Labeling law violations: fines from 0.5 to 100 UIT (up to ~PEN 525,000); selling non-compliant products: DIGESA product recall orders; repeated violations: suspension of market authorization
exceptions: Traditional ancestral foods (kiwicha, quinoa, cañihua in natural form) are exempt from octagonal labeling
Small artisanal producers below production thresholds have simplified registration
Exported foods must comply with destination country labeling rules, not Peruvian front-of-pack rules

quiz.q: What makes Peru particularly significant in global food biodiversity?
options: Home to over 3,000 potato varieties and extraordinary crop diversity
Invented the modern food safety inspection system
quiz.explanation: Peru is considered one of the world's primary centers of agricultural biodiversity — home to over 3,000 native potato varieties (potatoes originated in the Andes), hundreds of corn cultivars, and unique Amazonian fruits, representing extraordinary genetic diversity critical to global food security.

laws.title: Peru Ley de Protección y Bienestar Animal
laws.subtitle: Peru criminalizes animal cruelty with imprisonment
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Ley 30407 (Ley de Protección y Bienestar Animal, 2016) is a comprehensive animal welfare law that criminalizes animal cruelty with imprisonment. The law covers domestic and wild animals in captivity. It prohibits cruel acts, unnecessary suffering, abandonment, animal fighting, and use of animals in entertainment that causes suffering. Peru also has Law 26311 for the conservation of endemic wildlife species. Animal experimentation is regulated through bioethics committees. Local ordinances in Lima add additional companion animal protections. Peru's significant biodiversity makes wildlife trafficking an additional concern governed by separate environmental laws.
laws.penalty: Animal cruelty imprisonment: 3–5 years; aggravated cruelty (death): 5–7 years; animal fighting: 3–5 years imprisonment + disqualification
exceptions: Livestock slaughter under SENASA oversight
Licensed hunting
Scientific research approved by ethics committees
Traditional Andean practices subject to interpretation

quiz.q: What is the imprisonment range for aggravated animal cruelty resulting in the animal's death under Peru's Ley 30407?
quiz.explanation: Under Peru's Ley 30407, aggravated animal cruelty that results in the death of the animal carries a penalty of 5 to 7 years imprisonment — one of the more severe penalties in Latin America for such offenses.

laws.title: Peru Family Code — Civil Union Debate and Traditional Framework
laws.subtitle: Peru's Supreme Court ruled for same-sex civil unions in 2022
laws.fullDescription: Peru's family law is governed by the Código Civil (1984) and the Código de los Niños y Adolescentes. Peru's constitutional and legal framework traditionally defines marriage as man-woman. However, Peru's Supreme Court ruled in a 2022 landmark case that same-sex civil unions have constitutional protection under the right to equality and non-discrimination — a significant judicial development. Peru's property regime: separation of property is the default for unmarried couples; married couples can choose between community property (sociedad de gananciales) or separation (separación de bienes). Divorce requires 2 years separation (consensual) or proof of fault. Peruvian family law has strong alimony provisions for economically vulnerable spouses.
laws.penalty: Civil enforcement through juzgados de familia; pension alimenticia enforced by court; civil detention possible for willful non-payment; domestic violence measures under Law 30364
exceptions: Capitulaciones matrimoniales (prenuptial agreement)
Pre-marital property
Sociedad de gananciales or separación de bienes optional

quiz.q: What did Peru's Supreme Court rule in 2022 regarding same-sex couples?
options: The court ruled same-sex civil unions have constitutional protection under equality rights
The court required Congress to legalize same-sex marriage within 90 days
The court upheld Peru's traditional marriage-only framework
quiz.explanation: Peru's Supreme Court issued a landmark 2022 ruling finding that same-sex civil unions have constitutional protection under the right to equality and non-discrimination — a significant judicial development in a country where the legislature had not acted on LGBTQ+ rights. The ruling created a pathway for recognition without legislative action.

laws.title: Peru Property Formalization & COFOPRI
laws.subtitle: Massive urban land titling program
laws.fullDescription: Peru implemented one of the world's most ambitious urban land titling programs through COFOPRI (Organismo de Formalizacion de la Propiedad Informal), inspired by economist Hernando de Soto's thesis in 'The Mystery of Capital.' Between 1996 and 2015, COFOPRI issued over 2 million property titles to squatter settlement residents (pueblos jovenes), theoretically giving them collateral for credit and formal market participation. The Civil Code (Decreto Legislativo 295) governs private property rights. Peru's constitution (Art. 70) guarantees inviolability of private property subject to public interest.
laws.penalty: Informal settlement residents gain full title through COFOPRI; expropriation requires prior payment
exceptions: Titling does not automatically guarantee access to mortgage credit
Traditional indigenous community lands protected separately
laws.source: Constitucion Politica Art. 70; D. Leg. 295; Ley 28687

quiz.q: What famous economist's work inspired Peru's COFOPRI property titling program?
quiz.explanation: Peru's COFOPRI program was inspired by Hernando de Soto's influential work 'The Mystery of Capital' (2000), which argued that the poor's major asset is informal property that lacks formal legal recognition.

laws.title: Peru Codigo de Proteccion y Defensa del Consumidor
laws.subtitle: Comprehensive consumer code and INDECOPI enforcement
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Codigo de Proteccion y Defensa del Consumidor (Law 29571/2010) established comprehensive consumer rights including a 7-day retraction right for distance sales, strict product liability, mandatory warranties, and prohibition of abusive practices. INDECOPI (Instituto Nacional de Defensa de la Competencia y de la Proteccion de la Propiedad Intelectual) is the enforcement agency, handling both competition law and consumer protection. INDECOPI has been active against telecoms, banks, and airlines — sectors generating the most consumer complaints. Servicio de Atención al Ciudadano provides free mediation. Peru's Ley de Prevencion y Combate del Lavado de Activos also protects consumers in financial services.
laws.penalty: INDECOPI fine: up to 450 UIT (approx. USD 600,000) per violation; product recall authority
exceptions: INDECOPI handles competition, consumer, and IP enforcement together
7-day retraction right for distance purchases

quiz.q: What unique combination of enforcement areas does Peru's INDECOPI cover?
options: Competition law, consumer protection, and intellectual property
quiz.explanation: Peru's INDECOPI (Instituto Nacional de Defensa de la Competencia y de la Proteccion de la Propiedad Intelectual) uniquely combines competition law, consumer protection, and intellectual property enforcement in a single agency — unusual even by international standards.

laws.title: Fujimori Trials — Human Rights Prosecutions
laws.subtitle: Conviction and pardon of Alberto Fujimori
laws.fullDescription: Former President Alberto Fujimori (1990-2000) was extradited from Chile in 2007 and convicted in 2009 by Peru's Supreme Court for human rights violations (Barrios Altos massacre, La Cantuta killings by the Grupo Colina death squad) and corruption — receiving 25 years in prison. Fujimori was the first former head of state convicted of human rights abuses by his own country's courts. President Kuczynski controversially pardoned Fujimori in 2017 (later overturned by Constitutional Tribunal). Fujimori died in September 2024.
laws.penalty: Crimes against humanity: 25 years imprisonment (Fujimori sentence). No statute of limitations.
exceptions: Constitutional Tribunal overturned the 2017 humanitarian pardon
Amnesty laws blocked by Inter-American Court rulings
Joint criminal enterprise doctrine applied to death squad commanders

quiz.q: In what year was Alberto Fujimori convicted by Peru's Supreme Court?
quiz.explanation: Alberto Fujimori was convicted by Peru's Supreme Court in April 2009 and sentenced to 25 years in prison for human rights violations (Barrios Altos and La Cantuta massacres) and corruption. He was the first former head of state convicted by his own country's courts for human rights abuses.

laws.title: Machu Picchu — UNESCO and Cultural Heritage
laws.subtitle: Law 28296 — National Cultural Heritage protection
laws.fullDescription: Peru's General Law on Cultural Heritage (Law 28296, 2004) and UNESCO World Heritage status (1983) protect Machu Picchu and hundreds of archaeological sites. The Ministry of Culture administers 13,000+ registered archaeological sites. Tourist management at Machu Picchu — one of the world's most visited sites — has been controversial, with limits on daily visitors (4,500/day since 2017) repeatedly debated. A 2023 airport near Chinchero was approved despite environmental concerns. The Qhapaq Ñan (Andean Road System) spans 6 countries.
laws.penalty: Looting or damaging cultural heritage: 3-8 years imprisonment + civil damages. Unauthorized excavation: same penalties.
exceptions: Scientific research with Ministry of Culture permits
Indigenous communities may access ancestral sites with registration
Emergency conservation works authorized without standard permits

quiz.q: How many archaeological sites are registered in Peru?
quiz.explanation: Peru has over 13,000 registered archaeological sites managed by the Ministry of Culture. Peru's extraordinary archaeological heritage includes Machu Picchu (UNESCO 1983), Chan Chan (UNESCO 1986), the Nazca Lines, and thousands of Inca, Moche, and other pre-Columbian sites.

laws.title: Canon Minero — Mining Revenue Distribution
laws.subtitle: Canon system distributes mining royalties to regions
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Canon system distributes 50% of income tax from mining, oil, gas, and fisheries to regional and local governments where resources are extracted. The canon minero has created wealth inequities — mineral-rich regions receive vastly more than others. The Cañariaco copper project and Tía María mine have faced years of community opposition and protests. Peru is the world's second-largest copper producer and top silver producer. Conflicts over mining are endemic — Peru uses the 'Conflictos Sociales' monitoring system (Defensoría del Pueblo) tracking hundreds of active conflicts.
laws.penalty: Illegal mining: 4-12 years imprisonment. Mining without environmental impact assessment: operations suspension, fines.
exceptions: Artisanal small-scale mining (MAPE) has formalization programs
Indigenous consultation required for projects in native communities
REINFO (informal miner registry) provides transitional status
laws.sourceLabel: Ministerio de Energía y Minas — Perú

quiz.q: What percentage of mining income tax does Peru's Canon system distribute to producing regions?
quiz.explanation: Peru's Canon Minero distributes 50% of the income tax paid by mining companies to regional governments (25%) and local municipalities (25%) in the extraction zone. This system was designed to compensate resource-extracting regions but has created significant fiscal disparities between mineral-rich and mineral-poor regions.

laws.title: Hoja de Coca — Coca Leaf Legal Status
laws.subtitle: DEVIDA — legal coca vs. cocaine distinction
laws.fullDescription: Peru is one of the world's largest coca leaf producers — along with Colombia and Bolivia. Coca leaf cultivation for traditional uses (chewing, mate de coca, religious ceremony) is legal. The government regulates legal coca cultivation through ENACO (National Coca Company). Coca destined for cocaine production is illegal, and DEVIDA (anti-drug commission) conducts eradication programs. Coca cultivation in the VRAEM (Apurímac, Ene, Mantaro River Valley) remains Peru's most active cocaine production area and has guerrilla (Sendero Luminoso remnants) presence.
laws.penalty: Illegal coca cultivation for drug production: 2-15 years. Cocaine trafficking: 15-35 years.
exceptions: ENACO-registered farmers may cultivate coca legally
Traditional coca use in Andean communities protected as cultural right
Decoca (dried coca leaf) export for pharmaceutical use permitted
laws.sourceLabel: DEVIDA — Comisión Nacional para el Desarrollo y Vida sin Drogas

quiz.q: What Peruvian company regulates legal coca leaf cultivation and commercialization?
quiz.explanation: ENACO (Empresa Nacional de la Coca) is the Peruvian state company that regulates, purchases, and commercializes legally grown coca leaf. Farmers who register with ENACO may grow coca for traditional and industrial uses. Coca grown outside ENACO's system is presumed to be destined for cocaine production.

laws.title: Constitución 1993 — Fujimori's Constitution
laws.subtitle: 1993 constitution — still in force despite reform debate
laws.fullDescription: Peru's current 1993 Constitution was drafted after Fujimori's auto-coup (autogolpe) of April 1992, when he closed Congress and suspended the judiciary. A constituent assembly (Congreso Constituyente Democrático) wrote the new constitution, which enabled Fujimori's re-election and weakened institutional checks. Key changes from the 1979 constitution: single-chamber Congress, death penalty for terrorism, neo-liberal economic framework, reduced indigenous rights. Presidents Sagasti, Castillo, and Boluarte have all faced calls for constitutional reform.
laws.penalty: Constitutional violations: impeachment, criminal prosecution. Presidential violation of constitutional order: removal.
exceptions: Constitutional amendments require absolute majority + referendum (for certain articles) or two consecutive legislative periods
Eternity clauses protect some fundamental provisions
International human rights treaties have quasi-constitutional status

quiz.q: What triggered Peru's 1993 constitution — replacing the 1979 constitution?
options: A democratic referendum on constitutional reform
Fujimori's auto-coup (autogolpe) that closed Congress in 1992
A Supreme Court ruling invalidating the old constitution
quiz.explanation: Peru's 1993 Constitution resulted from Fujimori's autogolpe (self-coup) of April 5, 1992, when he unilaterally closed Congress, suspended the judiciary, and governed by decree. A new constituent assembly drafted the 1993 constitution, which included provisions enabling Fujimori's re-election and adopting neo-liberal economic policies.

laws.title: Esterilizaciones Forzadas — Forced Sterilization Victims
laws.subtitle: 1996-2000 forced sterilizations of indigenous women
laws.fullDescription: During Fujimori's government (1996-2000), approximately 270,000 women (mostly indigenous and poor) were sterilized through the Voluntary Surgical Contraception Program (AQV). Evidence indicates systematic coercion, deception, and force. Women were given quotas by health personnel under threat of losing social programs. Peru's Ministry of Justice created a registry (REVIESFO) for victims. Prosecutions have proceeded slowly — Fujimori's former health ministers faced charges. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights has maintained pressure on Peru to provide truth and reparations.
laws.penalty: State officials responsible: criminal prosecution for crimes against humanity (no statute of limitations).
exceptions: Reparations fund for victims regardless of criminal proceedings outcome
Health professionals who acted under coercion have some defenses
Evidentiary challenges given passage of time

quiz.q: Approximately how many women were sterilized under Peru's 1996-2000 forced sterilization program?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 270,000 women — mostly indigenous Quechua-speaking women and poor mestizas — were sterilized under the Fujimori government's Voluntary Surgical Contraception Program (AQV) between 1996-2000. Evidence shows systematic coercion and deception, with health workers given sterilization quotas.

laws.title: Pesca — Anchovy Fishing and Fishmeal Industry
laws.subtitle: Peru's anchovy fishery — world's largest by volume
laws.fullDescription: Peru has the world's largest single-species fishery — anchovy (anchoveta) from the cold Humboldt Current. Peru produces 30-35% of global fishmeal and fish oil, primarily for aquaculture feed in Asia and Europe. PRODUCE (Ministry of Production) manages individual vessel quotas (ITQ system). El Niño events dramatically reduce anchovy populations, causing major industry losses. The fishmeal industry generates $1.5+ billion annually. Direct human consumption of anchovy has been promoted through PRODUCE programs (anchoveta para el consumo humano directo).
laws.penalty: Fishing above quota: fines, vessel impoundment, license suspension. Fishing during closed season: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Artisanal boats (under 32.6 m³ hold) have separate artisanal fishery allocation
Scientific research vessels with permits
Sport fishing exempt from industrial quotas

quiz.q: What percentage of global fishmeal does Peru produce?
quiz.explanation: Peru produces 30-35% of global fishmeal, primarily from its anchovy (anchoveta) fishery. The cold Humboldt Current makes Peru's Pacific coast one of the world's most productive fisheries. Peruvian fishmeal is a primary feed ingredient in salmon and shrimp aquaculture globally.

laws.title: Ley Anticorrupción — Odebrecht Scandal
laws.subtitle: Lava Jato fallout — 4 former presidents under investigation
laws.fullDescription: Peru was severely impacted by the Odebrecht (Lava Jato) corruption scandal. The Brazilian construction company paid bribes to officials in all major Peruvian infrastructure projects. Presidents Alan García (died by suicide before arrest, 2019), Ollanta Humala, Pedro Pablo Kuczynski, and Alejandro Toledo (extradited from US) all faced investigation or prosecution. Peru's anti-corruption law framework was strengthened. Congress authorized a 'speedy trial' for corruption cases under Law 31161 (2021). The anti-corruption special prosecutor's office (ASPTP) was created.
laws.penalty: Public corruption: 5-10 years. Aggravated corruption (over 5 UIT involved): 10-15 years. Collusion with organized crime: up to 15 years.
exceptions: Presidential immunity during term (acusación constitucional required first)
Collaboration agreements (like in Lava Jato) reduce penalties for cooperating witnesses
Statute of limitations: 12-16 years for corruption offenses
laws.sourceLabel: Ministerio Público — Fiscalía de la Nación

quiz.q: Which Brazilian construction company at the center of the Lava Jato scandal paid bribes in Peru?
quiz.explanation: Odebrecht (now Novonor) was the Brazilian construction company at the center of the Lava Jato (Car Wash) scandal that implicated officials across Latin America. In Peru, Odebrecht paid bribes for major infrastructure contracts, implicating four former presidents: García, Humala, Kuczynski, and Toledo.

laws.title: Comunidades Campesinas — Indigenous Community Rights
laws.subtitle: Law 24656 — communal land and self-governance
laws.fullDescription: Peru has approximately 6,000 Comunidades Campesinas (Andean peasant communities) and 1,400 Comunidades Nativas (Amazon indigenous communities). Law 24656 (General Law of Peasant Communities, 1987) recognizes their legal personality, communal land (inalienable and imprescriptible), and self-governance through communal assemblies. Comunidades Nativas in the Amazon are governed by Decree Law 22175. ILO Convention 169 (ratified 1994) requires prior consultation. Land demarcation and titles remain incomplete for many communities, creating vulnerability to outside encroachment.
laws.penalty: Illegal occupation of communal lands: criminal prosecution. Failure to conduct required prior consultation: project suspension.
exceptions: Individual parcels within communities may be privately held under internal community rules
Communities may authorize temporary use of communal land by outsiders
Mining and oil projects on community land require both MINEM and consultation approval

quiz.q: Approximately how many Comunidades Campesinas (peasant communities) exist in Peru?
quiz.explanation: Peru has approximately 6,000 Comunidades Campesinas (Andean peasant communities) with recognized legal personality and communal land rights. Additionally, about 1,400 Comunidades Nativas (Amazon indigenous communities) exist. Together, these communities control significant portions of Peru's territory.

laws.title: Transporte Público — Lima's Metropolitano
laws.subtitle: BRT system and informal transport regulation
laws.fullDescription: Lima, one of the world's most congested cities, has reformed public transport through the Metropolitano BRT (Bus Rapid Transit, 2010) and Lima Metro Line 1 (2011). However, thousands of informal 'combis' (minivans) continue to operate. Peru's General Transport Law (Law 27181) regulates road transport. Lima's transport reform has been slow — informal operators resist formalization. The Metropolitan Municipality of Lima regulates urban transport. Accidents involving informal transport are frequent — Peru has high road fatality rates.
laws.penalty: Operating unlicensed public transport: vehicle confiscation, operator fines. Fare overcharging: administrative penalties.
exceptions: Rural transport in remote areas has simplified licensing
Special school transport vehicles have separate certification
Emergency transport during disasters has modified requirements

quiz.q: What type of public transit system is Lima's Metropolitano?
quiz.explanation: Lima's Metropolitano, opened in 2010, is a Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) system featuring dedicated bus lanes, prepaid boarding, and articulated buses. It serves hundreds of thousands of daily riders along its north-south corridor.

laws.title: Banco de la Nación — State Banking
laws.subtitle: State bank for government operations and rural banking
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Banco de la Nación (BN) provides government banking services and serves as a bank for citizens in areas without private bank access. BN operates in over 1,800 towns — critical for delivering social programs (Juntos, Pensión 65) to poor and rural populations. The Central Reserve Bank (BCRP) is independent and targets 2% inflation (±1%). Peru's financial system is dollarized — significant transactions occur in USD despite the sol (PEN). Peru's banking penetration remains relatively low (~50%) despite banking reforms.
laws.penalty: Financial fraud in state banking: criminal prosecution. Money laundering: 8-15 years.
exceptions: Microfinance institutions (Cajas Municipales) serve SMEs under separate SBS regulation
Cooperatives have modified banking requirements
Digital wallets (billeteras digitales) expanding financial inclusion

quiz.q: Peru's Banco de la Nación plays a key role in delivering which type of government programs?
quiz.explanation: Peru's Banco de la Nación is the primary channel for delivering social cash transfer programs including Juntos (for poor families) and Pensión 65 (for elderly poor). BN's presence in over 1,800 towns — including areas without private banks — is essential for financial inclusion and social program delivery.

laws.title: Amazonía Peruana — Amazon Conservation
laws.subtitle: SERNANP — 17% of Peru's territory in protected areas
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Amazon basin covers 60% of national territory and is home to extraordinary biodiversity. SERNANP (National Protected Areas Service) administers over 75 protected areas covering 17% of Peru's territory. Key areas: Manu National Park (UNESCO), Pacaya-Samiria (largest Amazonian reserve in Peru), Alto Mayo. SERFOR manages forest concessions outside protected areas. Peru has experienced significant deforestation — second in annual Amazon deforestation after Brazil — driven by agriculture, coca, and mining. Peru has committed to ending deforestation under climate agreements.
laws.penalty: Deforestation in protected areas: 3-5 years imprisonment, fines. Forest concession violations: permit revocation, fines.
exceptions: Native communities may practice subsistence use in buffer zones
Scientific research with SERNANP permits
Traditional Amazonian indigenous peoples' territory managed under AIDESEP
laws.sourceLabel: SERNANP — Sistema Nacional de Áreas Naturales Protegidas

quiz.q: What percentage of Peru's territory is covered by SERNANP-administered protected areas?
quiz.explanation: SERNANP administers over 75 protected areas covering approximately 17% of Peru's national territory. Combined with indigenous territories and forest concessions, much of Peru's Amazon basin has some form of land use regulation, though enforcement remains challenging.

laws.title: RENIEC — National Identity Registry
laws.subtitle: Documento Nacional de Identidad — universal registration
laws.fullDescription: Peru's RENIEC (Registro Nacional de Identificación y Estado Civil) issues the DNI (Documento Nacional de Identidad), mandatory for all Peruvians over 18. RENIEC's biometric DNI system is among Latin America's most advanced. Birth registration challenges affect remote Amazon communities — an estimated 10% of children lack birth certificates. RENIEC operates Mobile Registration Units in remote areas. The DNI is required for voting, banking, social programs, and most official transactions. Peru's electoral roll is automatically updated based on DNI registration.
laws.penalty: Failure to register civil acts (birth, marriage, death): administrative fines. Identity document fraud: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Newborns have 30 days for birth registration without penalty
Remote jungle communities have extended registration periods
Foreign residents have CE (Carné de Extranjería) instead of DNI

quiz.q: What document does Peru's RENIEC issue to all citizens over 18?
quiz.explanation: RENIEC issues the Documento Nacional de Identidad (DNI) — Peru's national identity card required for voting, banking, accessing social programs, and most official transactions. RENIEC's biometric DNI system is among Latin America's most technologically advanced.

laws.title: Vacancia Presidencial — Presidential Removal
laws.subtitle: Constitution Article 113 — 'moral incapacity' removal
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Constitution allows Congress to remove the president for 'moral incapacity' (Article 113(2)) — a vague provision used repeatedly. President Kuczynski was forced to resign under vacancia threat (2018). President Vizcarra was removed by Congress (2020, impeached twice). President Castillo tried to dissolve Congress illegally (December 2022) and was immediately removed and arrested. Peru has had 5 presidents in 5 years (2016-2021). The Constitutional Tribunal has ruled on the limits of vacancia, finding some uses unconstitutional.
laws.penalty: Abuse of vacancia procedure by Congress: constitutional court challenge. Presidential actions preceding vacancia: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Presidents retain immunity for acts done in exercise of presidential functions
Vacancia requires absolute majority (87 votes of 130)
Constitutional Tribunal may review vacancia declarations

quiz.q: Peru has used what constitutional provision repeatedly to remove presidents?
quiz.explanation: Peru's Constitution Article 113(2) allows Congress to declare the presidency vacant for 'moral incapacity' — a vague, undefined term. This provision has been used repeatedly in political crises, including the removals of Presidents Vizcarra (2020) and Castillo (2022), and the forced resignation of Kuczynski (2018).

laws.title: AFP Pensiones — Pension System Withdrawals
laws.subtitle: COVID withdrawals depleted individual retirement accounts
laws.fullDescription: Peru's AFP (private pension fund) system, similar to Chile's, requires 10% salary contributions. During COVID-19, Peru allowed extraordinary withdrawals — multiple rounds permitted workers to withdraw large portions of their AFP accounts. By 2022, approximately 3.8 million of Peru's 8 million AFP affiliates had zero balances. The withdrawals depleted retirement savings but provided immediate liquidity during the crisis. The SBS (Superintendency of Banks) oversees AFPs. Reforms to increase AFP coverage to informal workers remain a major policy challenge.
laws.penalty: AFP fraud: criminal prosecution. Late employer contributions: interest + penalties from SBS.
exceptions: Extraordinary withdrawal programs required congressional authorization
Workers who retired during COVID may have accessed full balance
Complementary public pension system (ONP) for older workers
laws.sourceLabel: Superintendencia de Banca, Seguros y AFP

quiz.q: By 2022, approximately how many Peruvian AFP affiliates had zero balances after COVID withdrawals?
quiz.explanation: By 2022, approximately 3.8 million of Peru's 8 million AFP pension fund affiliates had zero balances after multiple extraordinary withdrawal authorizations during COVID-19. While the withdrawals provided immediate economic relief, they severely depleted the retirement savings of millions of Peruvians.

laws.title: Ley de Salud Mental — Mental Health Law
laws.subtitle: Law 30947 (2019) — mental health rights
laws.fullDescription: Peru's Law 30947 (2019) establishes mental health as a public health priority and human right. It mandates community-based mental health care (Centros de Salud Mental Comunitarios), prohibits unjustified hospitalization, and establishes rights for people with mental health conditions. Peru has very limited mental health resources — 1.6 psychiatrists per 100,000 population (global average 1.7, developed countries 12+). The law was partly a response to the impact of political violence (Sendero Luminoso conflict, 1980-2000) on mental health. DEVIDA's programs also address trauma from drug-related violence.
laws.penalty: Involuntary hospitalization without legal grounds: civil liability, administrative sanctions. Discrimination based on mental health: Law 26772 applies.
exceptions: Emergency involuntary treatment for imminent danger allowed with court order
Research involving persons with mental illness requires enhanced consent procedures
Traditional Andean healing practices may complement clinical care

quiz.q: How many psychiatrists per 100,000 population does Peru have?
quiz.explanation: Peru has approximately 1.6 psychiatrists per 100,000 population — slightly below the global average of 1.7 and far below developed country levels of 12+. This severe shortage of mental health professionals limits implementation of Peru's progressive 2019 Mental Health Law.

laws.title: VRAEM — Drug Trafficking Control Zone
laws.subtitle: Apurímac-Ene-Mantaro Valley — military-controlled coca region
laws.fullDescription: The VRAEM (Valle de los Ríos Apurímac, Ene y Mantaro) is Peru's most troubled region — producing 60% of Peru's cocaine. Shining Path (Sendero Luminoso) remnants (now known as 'Militarized Communist Party') operate there providing armed protection to drug traffickers. Peru's military presence (VRAEM Emergency Zone) gives security forces special detention and search powers. Eradication programs face community resistance from coca farmers. The US provides counter-narcotics assistance through DEVIDA. An estimated 80,000 families depend on coca cultivation in the region.
laws.penalty: Cocaine trafficking from VRAEM: 15-25 years. Material support to armed groups: 20-35 years.
exceptions: ENACO-registered farmers may grow legal coca quantities
Community development programs for alternative crops (cacao, coffee)
Emergency zone restrictions may be suspended in periods of improved security
laws.sourceLabel: CORAH — Control y Reducción del Cultivo de Coca

quiz.q: What percentage of Peru's cocaine production comes from the VRAEM region?
quiz.explanation: The VRAEM (Valle de los Ríos Apurímac, Ene y Mantaro) produces approximately 60% of Peru's cocaine. The region is also the stronghold of Shining Path remnants who provide armed protection to drug trafficking operations. An estimated 80,000 families in the VRAEM depend on coca cultivation.

laws.title: El Niño — Climate Adaptation Law
laws.subtitle: Peru's vulnerability to ENSO cycles and climate disasters
laws.fullDescription: Peru is among the world's most vulnerable countries to El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events. The 1997-98 El Niño caused $3.5 billion in damages. Peru's National Meteorology Institute (SENAMHI) monitors ENSO. Law 29664 (2011) created SINAGERD (National Disaster Risk Management System) and CENEPRED/INDECI for prevention and response. The 2017 'Niño Costero' (coastal El Niño) caused catastrophic flooding in northern Peru. Peru's loss and damage was central to the COP27 climate negotiations.
laws.penalty: Failure by local governments to implement disaster risk plans: administrative responsibility. Building in high-risk zones: construction permit nullification.
exceptions: Emergency declarations allow expedited procurement
Indigenous disaster preparedness knowledge may inform official plans
International humanitarian aid has simplified entry procedures
laws.sourceLabel: INDECI — Instituto Nacional de Defensa Civil

quiz.q: What is the name of the 2011 Peruvian law that created the national disaster risk management system?
quiz.explanation: Peru's Law 29664 (2011) created SINAGERD (Sistema Nacional de Gestión del Riesgo de Desastres) and established CENEPRED (for risk reduction planning) and INDECI (for emergency response). The law was a response to Peru's high vulnerability to El Niño events, earthquakes, and floods.

laws.title: PROMPERÚ — Tourism Promotion
laws.subtitle: Commission for Tourism Promotion — Machu Picchu brand
laws.fullDescription: Peru's PROMPERÚ (Commission for the Promotion of Peru for Export and Tourism) promotes tourism internationally. Peru's 'Marca Perú' branding has been internationally acclaimed. Tourism generates $4+ billion annually, centered on Machu Picchu, Cusco, Lake Titicaca, the Amazon, and Lima's gastronomy. Lima's culinary scene (Central, Astrid y Gastón) has made Peru a global food destination. Tourism to Machu Picchu is managed with daily visitor limits. The Inca Trail requires advance booking months ahead. Peruvian gastronomy (ceviche, causa, lomo saltado) has obtained cultural heritage status.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized tourism operations in protected areas: fines, activity suspension. False tourism advertising: INDECOPI consumer protection actions.
exceptions: Community tourism initiatives in indigenous areas have simplified permits
Scientific expeditions have special entry permits for protected areas
Emergency closures of tourist sites compensated through insurance programs
laws.sourceLabel: PROMPERÚ — Comisión de Promoción del Perú

quiz.q: Peru's gastronomy has been recognized globally — which UNESCO status has Peruvian culinary culture received?
quiz.explanation: Lima was designated a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy in 2019. Peruvian gastronomy — including ceviche, causa, and lomo saltado — has been recognized for its cultural significance. Peruvian culinary innovations have made Lima a global food destination, with restaurants like Central appearing on World's 50 Best lists.

laws.title: Alianza del Pacífico — Pacific Alliance
laws.subtitle: Peru co-founder of Pacific Alliance economic bloc
laws.fullDescription: Peru is a founding member of the Pacific Alliance (Alianza del Pacífico), established in 2011 with Chile, Colombia, and Mexico. The bloc promotes free movement of goods, services, capital, and people among members. Peru has eliminated tariffs on 92%+ of trade with Pacific Alliance partners. The MILA (Integrated Latin American Market) links the stock exchanges of Lima, Santiago, Bogotá, and Mexico City. Pacific Alliance combined GDP is $2+ trillion — the 8th largest economy if a country. Peru uses the Pacific Alliance framework for trade negotiations and has observer status arrangements with 60+ countries.
laws.penalty: Tariff fraud within Pacific Alliance: customs penalties, goods confiscation, criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Agricultural products have transition periods for full tariff elimination
Rules of origin requirements must be met for preferential tariffs
Some services sectors are liberalized gradually

quiz.q: What year was the Pacific Alliance (Alianza del Pacífico) established?
quiz.explanation: The Pacific Alliance was established in 2011 by Chile, Colombia, Mexico, and Peru. It promotes free movement of goods, services, capital, and people. Combined, the four member countries represent the 8th largest economy globally with a GDP of over $2 trillion.
